#3160. Warren Buffett's Successor, Greg Abel, Just Bought $9.6 Billion of the Oracle of Omaha's Favorite Stock (No, Not Alphabet!)

Since mid-2018, Buffett and Abel have deployed roughly $92 billion of Berkshire Hathaway’s capital into a company near and dear to the Oracle of Omaha’s heart.

Few events garner more attention on Wall Street than Berkshire Hathaway's (BRKA +2.60%)(BRKB +1.41%) earnings reports. This is especially true now that Warren Buffett has retired and his successor, Greg Abel, is overseeing the company's day-to-day operations and its closely watched $359 billion investment portfolio.

While the September-ended quarter was more or less business as usual for the trillion-dollar conglomerate that Buffett built, with Berkshire recording $12.7 billion in operating earnings, another figure stole the show. Namely, a $9.6 billion purchase of the Oracle of Omaha's favorite stock by Abel.

The Oracle of Omaha's favorite stock is back on the menu. Image source: Getty Images.

Through the first half of 2026, Abel's headline buy was Google parent Alphabet (GOOGL -0.27%)(GOOG -0.38%). While Buffett initiated the position in Alphabet before his retirement, it was Abel who grew it into a top-three holding at one point. Berkshire's new boss has put tech on the menu in a way that wasn't seen under Buffett.

But it wasn't a tech purchase that raised eyebrows in the third quarter. In fact, you won't even find evidence of this purchase in Berkshire Hathaway's quarterly Form 13F, which should be filed on Nov. 16.

In Berkshire's third-quarter operating results, on the final page before the executive certifications, the company details Abel's purchase activity in the stock Buffett holds nearest and dearest to his heart... Berkshire Hathaway.

BREAKING: Berkshire Hathaway more than doubled its stock buybacks in Q3 2026, repurchasing $9.6 billion of its own shares. This brings total buybacks in 2026 to $14.4 billion, marking a sharp reversal after the company paused repurchases for nearly 22 months. Berkshire also revealed that it has been a net buyer of stocks in 2026, with net purchases hitting +$11.2 billion YTD. This compares to net stock sales of -$10.6 billion over the same period in 2025. Berkshire is deploying capital again.

Between July 1 and Sept. 30, Abel oversaw the purchase of 4,536 Class A shares (BRKA) and 12,384,959 Class B shares (BRKA), totaling approximately $9.6 billion. This more than doubles the $4.53 billion spent on share buybacks in the second quarter and brings cumulative share repurchases between Buffett and Abel since mid-2018 to approximately $92 billion.

As long as Berkshire Hathaway has at least $30 billion in combined cash, cash equivalents, and U.S. Treasury bills on its balance sheet -- it closed out September 2026 with $377.4 billion -- and Abel believes the company's shares are intrinsically cheap, buybacks can be made with no end date or ceiling.

Since Berkshire Hathaway doesn't pay a dividend, buybacks are a direct way to reward its shareholders (in case a greater-than-6,000,000% outperformance of the S&P 500 since the mid-1960s wasn't enough). Buybacks encourage the long-term investing ethos that Buffett values and can incrementally increase investors' ownership stakes over time.

A hearty share repurchase program can also make a company's stock more attractive to fundamentally-focused investors. Companies with steady or growing net income and a declining outstanding share count, courtesy of an ongoing buyback program, should see earnings per share rise over time.

An aggressive share buyback program can also signal to Wall Street and investors that management sees value in their company's stock.

BRK.A Price to Book Value data by YCharts

Over Warren Buffett's final 19 months as CEO, as well as during Abel's first two months at the helm, not one penny was used for buybacks. During this 21-month period, Berkshire's stock predominantly traded at a 60% to 80% premium to its book value. Since mid-2018, Berkshire's bosses have consistently green-lit buybacks when its shares trade at less than a 50% premium to book value. For context, shares have oscillated between a 40% and 50% premium over the previous two quarters.

Even though Buffett and Abel have been decisive net sellers of stocks over the last four years, Buffett's favorite stock is clearly on the menu.

#3159. Thinking Machines’ new model takes the lead in western open-weight AI

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Another competitive model developed outside of China could change the open-weight landscape.

Thinking Machines Lab, a small AI startup from ex-OpenAI CTO Mira Murati, has released its latest model, Inkling 2 Small — and according to third-party tester Artificial Analysis, it’s set to give Chinese models a run for their lead. It’s technically proprietary until now, but Thinking Machines said it will release its weights next week.

Also: Open weights vs. closed: An AI civil war’s afoot

Chinese companies have led the pack on open models over the last few years. Models from DeepSeek and Moonshot regularly top leaderboards and rival the capabilities of much more expensive, closed models from OpenAI and Anthropic.

Since DeepSeek’s R1 performed similarly to OpenAI’s o1 in January 2025, Chinese open models have given investors and high-paying enterprise customers reasons to rethink their expensive contracts with US-based labs. Western labs creating more competitive open models changes the landscape.

Thinking Machines’ latest model has 594 billion parameters and supports image inputs but outputs only text. The company noted its web and game design capabilities and that it evaluated the model’s approach to coding problems alongside the code it generated during testing.

“The result is a model that is both stronger at coding and easier to use inside real agent loops,” the company said.

Also: Nvidia takes another step forward for US open-weight AI

Inkling 2 Small scored a 31 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, a composite test “for tracking progress toward artificial general intelligence” that combines benchmark scores spanning coding, science, and general categories. A score of 31 is above average for models in its class and is tied with Gemini 3.8 Flash. For context, Gemini 4 Carbon and Claude Opus 5.5 top the index at 60 and 59, respectively.

Thinking Machines said it will release the model’s weights next week, a practice that is becoming customary. Given the heightened security concerns around AI in general, AI companies spend a few weeks testing the to-be-open model with cybersecurity teams and safety reviewers before releasing the weights, rather than leading with the weights out of the gate.

French AI lab Mistral recently released its Le Chonk model via the same staggered process — it now keeps pace with OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Terra in coding abilities, which is rare for western-made open models.

Also: Mistral’s Le Chonk is now a top open model for coding

“[Thinking Machines’] plan to release its weights would make it the highest-scoring open weights model developed outside China based on current rankings,” Artificial Analysis said.

“Inkling 2 Small is amongst the leading models in intelligence and reasonably priced when comparing to other models of similar price. It’s also notably slow per task and very verbose,” Artificial Analysis said. The organization also called Inkling 2 Small’s pricing “somewhat expensive” at $0.30 per one million input tokens, since the median cost for its class is $0.24.

Still, the model’s progress over its predecessor stands out to Artificial Analysis reviewers: Inkling 2 Small jumped 41% in automation capabilities and 20% in coding abilities. However, most models excel in certain areas or on specific benchmarks, making it hard to deem one or another the outright best coding model overall.

Also: I tried replacing Claude Code with a local AI stack that’s completely free

Inkling 2 Small also made some gains in accuracy, Artificial Analysis said.

“On AA-Omniscience v1.1, the hallucination rate falls from Inkling Small’s 61% to 27%, while accuracy rises from 32% to 34% and the attempt rate falls from 77% to 53%,” its review reported.

Ring's $250 flying indoor security camera is set to arrive in January. We got a first look at the Drone Cam in action.

Ring Home Security has taken flight, and the brand’s tiny new home security drone is less expensive than we thought. The Ring Drone Cam, a $250 mini indoor drone camera, was announced on Tuesday as part of the brand’s new arm, Ring Robotics. It uses a learned map of your home to zoom around autonomously for up to 8 minutes at a time with custom routes to record places a couple of fixed cameras can’t.

The small drone weighs just 5.8 ounces and houses a pair of 2K-resolution cameras mounted on the front and bottom, respectively. The cameras use bright LED lights to enable day or night monitoring, sending a live feed or recorded video to your device. The LEDs are also meant to ward off potential intruders peering in from the outside.

You can program the flying cam to make regular flights or send it on specific missions to check on the dog or see if the stove was left on. The Drone Cam also syncs with other Ring cameras and sensors to respond automatically when windows and doors open at certain hours.

If you’re thinking, “Wait, didn’t Ring already launch a drone camera?” you’d be right — sort of. The brand “launched” the Ring Always Home Cam in 2020. The $250 indoor drone had a limited, invitation-only release but was never available for public sale. We’ve been assured this latest iteration is ready for prime time, though it’s still not available for preorder on Amazon.

Ring founder and CEO Jamie Siminoff demoed the drone, which has been in development for more than five years, in an event space set up to replicate a home. During the demo, the small drone lifted gently from the dock and rose to about eye level, where it hovered as if to say “hello” to the group of journalists gathered around.

Once airborne, the drone turned toward the adjacent room and whirred off to investigate. After a few seconds of scanning, the drone returned to the first room, docked and resumed charging.

While in flight, the Ring Drone Cam made a notably loud buzz reminiscent of a golf cart in reverse. Siminoff quickly noted that the sound was intentional, meant to deter potential intruders and alert home dwellers to the drone’s presence.

The 1-minute flight was enough to cover two medium-sized rooms, though the drone can fly up to eight minutes on a full charge before needing about an hour to recharge. Ring reps told me it can monitor a home up to 3,500 square feet – more than enough for most – but Siminoff says it plans to improve the range over time.

If you’re worried about the drone knocking over vases and flying into ceiling fans like I was, Siminoff assured us the preprogrammed coverage zone is tight.

The drone is powered by AI Pilot, “a custom-built system that uses the device’s cameras, specialized vision models, sensors and cloud processing to see, think, and navigate autonomously.” (We’ll see for ourselves once we get a unit in for testing.)

To create your drone’s fly zone, you carry it through the space where it intelligently identifies rooms and suggests patrol points like doors, windows or a nursery. You can add rooms and areas based on your home’s layout and security preferences.

The $250 Ring Drone Cam isn’t yet available for preorder, but Ring representatives at the launch event assured us it will be soon, and units are set to begin shipping in late January 2027. We’ll update this story when it becomes available for preorder or purchase.

#3154. Alpine Linux and OpenSSH patch flaw that’s as bad as it can get

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

This dangerous Linux security hole must be patched as soon as possible.

The perfect nightmare scenario for a Linux server is when all an attacker needs to do is reach the server’s Secure Shell (SSH) port, waltz right in, and take it over. That’s what happened to Alpine Linux, the popular, lightweight Linux server. Adding insult to injury, this happened only days after Alpine Linux dodged a security hole-sized bullet to its GitLab implementation.

Also: Linux Mint 27 arrives next month, and I like it already: What to expect

How bad is it? As bad as it can get. Alpine Linux explained in its security advisory that if an attacker can reach a vulnerable server’s SSH port, they can get in “with one connection,” and the attack “works every time, and needs no retries.”

As security engineer Gregory Bryant explained in his LinkedIn post:

Most authentication bypasses come from complex logic chains, but yesterday’s Alpine Linux OpenSSH vulnerability (CVE-2026-123158) comes down to a single character: *.”

If you run Alpine Linux (or another musl-based distro) with the default openssh-server package (no Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM)) and PasswordAuthentication enabled, an attacker can log into password-disabled, or key-only accounts simply by sending a password between 257 and 1024 bytes long.

Alpine Linux isn’t the only operating system that uses musl, a lightweight version of the standard C library (libc). Other operating systems that use musl and are potentially vulnerable include Adélie Linux; Void Linux; Sabotage Linux; OpenWrt, an Android variant,  and the Yocto Project, which is used to build embedded Linux distributions.

Also: This clever banking scam keeps phishing by faking its own demise

Wind River, which produces the commercial embedded Linux distro, Wind River Linux, is also looking into the issue. A company representative told me, “Wind River takes security seriously. We are actively reviewing the reported vulnerability and assessing its potential impact. We will take appropriate action as needed.”

Behind the scenes, when OpenSSH is built without PAM, it verifies passwords by hashing the password attempt using the C library’s crypt() function. It then compares the result to the account’s stored password field. So far, so good.

But when a key is longer than 256 bytes, musl’s crypt() function returns the string * as an error indicator. That is also what the password field holds for any account with no password, such as a key-only account. Thus, the “hash” matches and the login succeeds, and the attacker walks in.

Also: The new Cutefish Linux distro might be the best MacOS clone around

To exploit it, an attacker only needs the name of such an account. The attacker also needs at least one other account on the machine with a 5 or 6 password hash, and then to send a password of 257 to 1,024 bytes. According to Alpine, one user with a password is enough to make every passwordless account accessible.

In Linux systems that use glibc’s crypt(), which is almost all of them, the same attempt would return NULL on error, which sshd already rejects, so Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora, etc., aren’t affected.

According to *sshole, the group that uncovered the problem, this is a side effect that has been hiding since 2016.

Alpine said every release it checked is affected: 3.21 through 3.24, edge, and the older 3.16 to 3.20 branches. Exposure requires the following:

Root is not directly exposed in most cases. It has shipped as root:* in the base image since about Alpine 3.16, but OpenSSH’s default PermitRootLogin prohibit-password blocks it. Another account that can become root, for example through doas, still gives an attacker a route to root.

Alpine singled out its official tiny-cloud images, versions 3.18.11 through 3.24.3, as especially vulnerable. These ship with an alpine user with a * password field and passwordless doas. They are safe on first boot but become exploitable once any 6 hash exists on the machine. That can happen when an administrator sets a console password or when user data adds a user with a hashed password, which means, essentially, all of them.

Alpine released 3.21.10, 3.22.8, 3.23.8 and 3.24.4 on Thursday, with the OpenSSH fix among the security changes. It also published fixed packages for each release back to 3.16. Alpine 3.21 reached end of support on Nov. 1.

The just-released OpenSSH 10.6p2 avoids the problem in sshd. Alpine’s stable branches carry a patch for the same problem. You should run apk upgrade -U -a and then restart the daemon with rc-service sshd restart. Alpine stressed that upgrading the package does not replace the running daemon. Anyone who cannot update should set PasswordAuthentication no and restart sshd, after confirming that key login works.

Also: Maze Linux is the best security-focused distro I’ve ever tested

To check for an attack, Alpine told administrators to search /var/log/messages for “Accepted password for” lines that name an account with no password. It also advised reviewing dedicated OpenBSD application subexecutor (doas) use and recently created users, files, and authorized keys. “If you cannot rule out a login, treat the machine as compromised.” Just what you wanted for your weekend, I know, but here we are.

#3153. Adobe Is Giving Its AI Agents Even More to Do

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Across Firefly and Creative Cloud, apps are getting even deeper into creative work.

Would you use an always-on AI agent such as Claude Duet or OpenAI’s Dot to edit your photos? At Adobe Max on Tuesday, the company announced it’s expanding its local MCP integrations with more third-party companies to enable more autonomous creative work.

MCP, or Model Context Protocol, is an open-source protocol for connecting AI systems to external apps and databases. AI agents and MCPs act as a two-way street. Agents, or fancy bots, can complete tasks independently.

For example, if you wanted your OpenAI agents (or Dots, whatever you call them) to edit a project in Photoshop, the MCP pathway would allow ChatGPT to run agents to edit the design in the Photoshop beta desktop app — no need to search through the toolbar if you’re not familiar with it.

The new MCP integrations are in preview now. The idea is to give people more choice by letting them use their preferred AI app to help them work in select Creative Cloud apps.

Over the past year, Adobe has been working with AI companies to bring its creative knowledge and tech to ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Copilot as Adobe plugins. It’s also brought external models from AI companies into Firefly, Adobe’s AI hub. Now, Adobe is deepening its relationships with third-party AI vendors to adapt to the agentic AI era.

Bringing your own agents offers a degree of user control, according to Shilpa Anand, vice president of global strategic partnerships. “These new models allow me to actually do things faster, experience the full power of the application and really make it more accessible to a broader set of users who are not experts in our workflow,” Anand told me.

Agentic AI has been a huge focus for tech companies this year. It’s the next step for companies that want to move beyond mere chat and information-gathering AI capabilities.

Adobe has been driving toward this vision for a while. It released AI assistants in Photoshop and Adobe Express that set the foundation for June’s official launch of Adobe creative agents.

But AI agents from frontier labs such as OpenAI and Anthropic caused trouble this summer when they escaped testing environments and hacked real websites. Anand told me that safety and security are “table stakes” for Adobe and that there haven’t been any issues aligning with other AI companies on safety precautions.

When considering partnerships, the company also considers which AI models will be most useful for Adobe’s creative customers, which is why Firefly includes models from big players including Google, as well as more specialized AI companies, such as ElevenLabs for AI audio tech. (Adobe acquired Topaz Labs, which makes AI photo editing software, earlier this year.)

Those creative AI agents are getting new capabilities across Creative Cloud apps, too. In Firefly, the company’s AI hub, its AI assistant should now be better at multistep or more complex tasks, and it has a new “plan mode” in preview that lets you review the agent’s plan before it starts running.

New “always-on” Firefly AI agents do exactly what the name implies: They’re always working and can handle predefined tasks, such as assessing image quality in new asset uploads. They’re in preview now, too. And across Illustrator, InDesign, Premiere, After Effects and Frame.io, those AI assistants are getting upgraded capabilities as well.

Adobe is also expanding its partnerships. Microsoft Photos will have a built-in Adobe Express integration, and Microsoft’s Arm-based Windows PCs are getting “optimized” Adobe apps. Disney is also deepening its relationship with Adobe, bringing Adobe’s Firefly AI tech to its creative teams.

Partnerships with AI companies and the integration of agentic capabilities will continue to be a focus for Adobe next year, Anand told me. “Agentic software is really going to enable us to reach more users and empower everyone to create, which is our mission.”

As anticipated, we recognized a $2.6 million benefit from IEEPA tariff refunds as a reduction in cost of sales. Cultivation and Gardening accounted for the increase in gross profit with segment gross profit up $1.7 million or 18.4%. In addition to the IEEPA refunds, a higher mix of proprietary brand sales helped margin. Lower sales from a smaller footprint for our stores weighed on gross profit, while pricing pressure, higher transportation costs and higher estimated inventory obsolescence costs weighed on margin. In Storage Solutions, gross profit dollars were essentially unchanged, although segment margin declined modestly. Turning to expenses. Total operating expenses declined 7.1% to $14.6 million from $15.7 million a year ago.

Store and other operating expenses fell 11.9% to $6.4 million from $7.2 million, reflecting our smaller store footprint. SG&A increased to $6.8 million from $5.7 million, driven by higher commercial sales-related spending and one-time charges incurred during the quarter. Depreciation and amortization totaled $1.2 million, down $1.5 million or 55.2% compared to $2.6 million in the same period last year. The decrease primarily reflects asset retirements related to cost reduction initiatives and certain intangible assets reaching the end of their useful lives. GAAP net income was $0.2 million, a $2.7 million improvement compared to a net loss of $2.4 million or negative $0.04 per share in the prior year period.

The improvement was primarily driven by higher gross margin, including the tariff refund benefit and lower operating expenses, partially offset by lower sales volume. In the third quarter, we delivered our second consecutive quarter of positive adjusted EBITDA. Non-GAAP adjusted EBITDA, as defined in our press release, was $2.3 million, a $1 million year-over-year improvement compared to $1.3 million in the prior year. Now turning to the balance sheet. We ended the quarter with $41.8 million of cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities and no debt. We continue to maintain a debt-free balance sheet. Our cash position gives us the financial flexibility to invest in organic growth, evaluate strategic opportunities and opportunistically return capital to shareholders.

We also returned approximately $1 million to shareholders during the quarter, repurchasing 700,000 shares at an average price of $1.46 per share, excluding transaction costs. We did so while preserving the liquidity we need to fund operations and invest in the business. At quarter end, approximately $8 million remained available for future repurchase. As Darren outlined, we are narrowing our full year revenue guidance to $163 million to $165 million. We are also withdrawing our previous adjusted EBITDA guidance of $2 million to $3 million due to the actions we are now taking to lower our ongoing cost base and position GrowGeneration for greater profitability in 2027.

While the store closures and other restructuring activities will affect our fourth quarter results, we expect the resulting savings and operating efficiencies to strengthen our financial performance in the year ahead. That said, we're satisfied with our third quarter results and with our performance through September, which was ahead of our initial plan for the year. We ended the quarter with $41.8 million in cash, cash equivalents, marketable securities and no debt. We have the financial flexibility to carry out our fourth quarter initiatives while continuing to invest in the business. We believe these actions position us to extend our multiyear track record of improving profitability heading into 2027.

With that, I'll turn the call back to Darren for closing remarks.

Darren Lampert: Thanks, Greg, and thank you again to everyone for joining us today. In closing, the most important takeaway today is that GrowGeneration is a fundamentally different business from what we were several years ago. We have substantially transitioned from a retail-centric hydroponic business into a national commercial cultivation supply and proprietary brand platform. We've expanded our proprietary brands, reduced operating expenses and improved profitability. And we've accomplished this while maintaining a strong balance sheet with no debt. Our third quarter results demonstrate the progress we've already made to building a stronger, more profitable company that generates sustainable cash flow and creates long-term value for our shareholders. I want to thank our employees, customers, vendors and stakeholders for their continued support.

That concludes our prepared remarks. Operator, please open the line for questions

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Your first question comes from Aaron Grey from Alliance Global Partners.

Aaron Grey: So first question for me, just if you could quantify the expected savings from the initiative expected to be completed in 2026. So how should we think about 2027 from a margin structure and profitability given that's what this initiative will be setting up for?

Greg Sanders: Yes. Thanks for the question, Aaron. So far, we're encouraged with the performance in 2026. We've brought the business from a $14 million adjusted EBITDA loss in '24 to a $6 million adjusted EBITDA loss last year and this year, we're at $1 million profit through the first 3 quarters. And we see an opportunity to reposition the business for heightened profitability next year. We are working through the restructuring plan right now. We intend to close 2 to 3 additional locations yet this quarter. We've already closed 2, so we're already underway. We are looking at other rationalizations across the company, including inventory charges that may occur in the fourth quarter.

So at this point, obviously, we dropped the EBITDA guidance with just the uncertainty around Q4 specifically, but we are aiming to complete most of the actions this quarter. There may be some additional actions that trail into the first quarter of 2027. Overall, we expect the resulting actions to meaningfully improve profitability in 2027. As we finalize our restructuring accounting, we will issue an 8-K with an update on how we see the incremental improvement translating into our results next year.

Aaron Grey: Okay. So if not able to quantify now, I guess, maybe taking it a different way, the stores that you are closing, the 4 to 5, those were weighing on the margin now. So getting out of those, and I know there might be some leases you might be able to get out as well. It's fair to say those were a drag on profitability currently and will be accretive once you get through the respective inventory of those stores, which might take 4Q into 1Q next year?

Darren Lampert: I think, Aaron, when you take a look at it, this will be -- we've closed 10 stores since the third quarter last year. Adding the additional 4 stores in the fourth quarter will be down 14 stores from Q3 last year. Each store closing certainly goes with cost savings, both from store employees, lease, and it funnels down to back-office staff and everything that goes into running these stores. When you start taking a look at the EBITDA guidance that we're giving where we started a couple of years ago, back in 2024, we lost about $16.5 million on an adjusted basis.

We lost $6 million last year and most likely going to be profitable this year or [ positive ] through the third quarter. So I think it's the whole show. You're talking about transportation, you're talking about distribution costs, you're talking about warehousing costs, inventory costs, inventory obsolescence costs. So I think when you take the whole picture as a whole and where we've come in the last couple of years going from $16 million in 2024 on the loss side to, again, we're positive $1 million this year right now. I think you can kind of look where the future is going.

We've been pretty transparent with Wall Street with the store closings and going to a B2B business, growing proprietary brands, which is over 40% right now and with margins increasing and expenses going down. So we are right now because everything is working, we're accelerating what we've been doing over the last 5 years. And I think this is probably one of the -- probably getting to the end of it. But what we're seeing right now is all positive. And so we're accelerating to get where we need to get.

Operator: Your next question comes from Brian Nagel from Oppenheimer.

Brian Nagel: So I think my question is going to be a follow-up to the prior question, but more -- maybe more qualitative. But with this -- the actions you're taking now in the fourth quarter, what spurred this? Is there something specific you saw in the business that caused you to take what seems to be more aggressive actions? And then I'll have a follow-up.

Darren Lampert: I think, Brian, a couple of different things. One, when changing business models from a retailer from a business to consumer to a business to business, there's certainly a lot to be done. And what we're seeing within the business right now is the business-to-business is working, the business-to-consumer is not. The traffic within the stores are just not there. So we're pretty much refining. We're changing the business as we've done over the last 5 years. There's nothing that is really pushing what we're doing right now. But as you know, costs are going up, transportation costs are going up, distribution costs are going up, container pricing are going up right now.

And I think we're just being very proactive, but we're being proactive into strength. The business is working. And we do believe that there's a lot of expenses that we can still take out of this business. And I think it starts with the stores. When you take the store business out within the store business, the purchasing team gets a little lighter. The supply chain gets lighter. Every component of the cost center of the business drops. And that's what we're working on right now. We were able to get rid of some leases. We paid to get out of some leases.

But when you look last year, as I said earlier, third quarter of 2025, we'll be down 14 stores from then. And you see it's not really impacting the -- you're not really impacting our sales nor our profitability. Our profitability is going up and our sales are pretty much staying the same. And I think we've been pretty transparent that we close stores, we do lose a bunch of walk-in business. we're picking up on the commercial side, and we're picking it up on our proprietary brand side and also our wholesale side. So most of the business is working. The stores are not.

Brian Nagel: That's very helpful, Darren. So I guess just a clarification on that. So as we think about the actions you're taking here in the fourth quarter, that's primarily more aggressively closing a larger number of stores?

Darren Lampert: Again, we're going from -- I think we're going from 19 down to 14. So on a percentage basis is a pretty high number. We still do use some stores for distribution. You'll probably see another couple of store closings next year, but they won't be -- you won't see 5 in 1 quarter. When you go back to last year, we closed, I think, 7 in the third quarter last year and 4 in the fourth quarter last year. So we've been closing pretty quickly. We started with 65 stores back in 2022. So we'll be down from 65 stores down to 14 by the end of this year.

Brian Nagel: Okay. And then my final question, just with regard to the guidance. So it sounds like you're going to have -- you'll have -- if I'm understanding correctly, you'll have extra expenses now in this fourth quarter given these restructuring actions. So when you report fourth quarter results, will you be able to basically articulate how much of the results are kind of one-time in nature, reflecting these more aggressive restructuring actions versus the ongoing operations of the business?

Greg Sanders: Yes, that's exactly right, Brian. Our aim with this action that we're taking in the fourth quarter, it may extend slightly into the first as well is to quantify the total impact and include the forward-looking guidance in 2027 reflective of the improvements that we believe we can make and execute in this window of time to better position the company for that continued track record of improved profitability that we've delivered the last several years into 2027 and beyond.

Operator: Your next question comes from Mark Smith from Lake Street.

Mark Smith: Curious, first off, just as we continue to transition more to B2B business here, any call-outs on customer concentration or increased risk that you run there?

Greg Sanders: I was going to say we -- as a company, Mark, and it's a very good question, are still very diversified from a customer perspective. There are no customers in our portfolio that account for more than 5% of sales today. When we close stores, we aim to retain all of the commercial customers that shop in that general market or region through another closely approximated store or through our commercial sales team. So from a concentration perspective, we feel that these moves don't present a significant amount of risk from a retention perspective given the diversified nature of our customer base across the portfolio.

Mark Smith: Okay. And then just curious if you can give us just an update on your view of the industry and if you've seen any kind of tailwinds develop as we've moved into rescheduling?

Darren Lampert: I think right now, Mark, it's going to be some time and people are still awaiting rescheduling on adult use still in front of the ALJ and people are expecting a decision within -- hopefully within -- by the end of the year, but which keeps getting pushed back. But I think people are still waiting. Our business has been relatively strong. Again, we've closed 14 stores. It will be 14 stores in the last year, and we do lose business when we close stores. So if you took the store closures out, we'd have quite an increase year-over-year on a sales basis.

But again, we're certainly making that back on the other side of it by cutting expenses and growing proprietary brands. Our proprietary brands were up 19% year-over-year in a difficult market. So we believe you'll see a lot of consolidation on an ongoing basis. And the larger customers want to deal with a company that can handle their needs from a financing side, from a product side of it and others from a technical side of it. We have built a pretty incredible technical team at GrowGen and a commercial sales team at GrowGen. And it is certainly helping keep the customers as we close stores.

And one of the main -- when we take a look at what stores we're closing, it's the stores that have mostly commercial customers that we can service with our commercial team and service through drop shipping from our warehouses. It's not the stores that have -- that still do have customer walk-ins. So we do still have a number of stores where the -- where customers are coming to the stores, shopping at the stores. Those stores we will keep for a while. There's no reason to close some of them. We still do have some profitable stores within the portfolio.

But the other side is when we close stores, we are getting rid of back-office staff and really cutting down the expenses of this company. I think you guys will be quite happy when you hear what we've done within the fourth quarter on really trimming expenses of this company really without trimming sales forecast for next year. So we're excited to go into 2027, and we certainly hope cleaner than we've gone into any other year since 2021.

Operator: There are no further questions at this time. I will turn the call back over to Darren for closing remarks.

Darren Lampert: Thank you. I want to once again thank our employees, customers, vendors and stakeholders for their continued support in GrowGeneration. I want to wish everybody a happy holiday season, and we look forward to updating everybody with our fourth quarter and year-end numbers in March. And hopefully, we'll have some news out before then. Thank you.

Operator: Ladies and gentlemen, this concludes today's conference call. You may now disconnect. Thank you.

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Galaxy device owners who are heavy AI users would likely start paying for some features they've long enjoyed for free.

Samsung is reportedly planning a shift from free unlimited Galaxy AI tools to a tiered subscription plan. This would be a major adjustment for Galaxy device owners who are heavy AI users, as they’d likely have to pay for some features they’ve long enjoyed for free.

Also: 7 Samsung Galaxy settings I always change

Tools like Photo Assist, Now Brief, and Creative Studio will still remain free, according to reports — they just won’t offer unlimited usage. Once the allotted number of free credits runs out, Samsung plans to introduce either standalone packages to top up AI credits or a monthly or annual subscription for users to continue using these features.

No free usage limit has been specified for users, but the highest-tiered subscription claims to offer usage limits four times higher than the free plan. A subscription would also give users access to exclusive features, presumably high-compute and newer processes.

The Galaxy AI Premium subscription would start at $4.99 per month or $47.99 per year, and reports indicate it would go up from there.

Samsung is planning to roll out a paid subscription model for the Galaxy S27 series, according to code references in 2027 Samsung devices. The company is reportedly planning to expand the plan to older devices through One UI updates, including S24 series models and newer devices, as well as Fold and Flip series phones.

If you’re an occasional Galaxy AI user, you probably won’t ever need to pay to use your preferred AI features. This would include those who edit a photo or summarize an email every now and then.

Power users and those who rely heavily on Galaxy AI daily will need to decide whether yet another subscription is worth the money. Aside from a higher token limit, these features would include AI-generated videos, Bixby Action, and Daily Briefing.

Samsung hasn’t announced a release date for the Galaxy S27 Series phones, but the company typically holds a Galaxy Unpacked event in January or February.

#3148. Samsung’s new SmartTag 3 debuts with next-gen Bluetooth – and one big problem

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

The Galaxy SmartTag 3 supports emerging Bluetooth tracking tech, but it's not a match for Samsung's OS exclusivity.

Samsung’s Galaxy SmartTag 3 is now available for purchase in the US, promising a smaller, lighter design than previous generations, compatibility with iOS devices, 550 days of battery life, an NFC-powered Lost Mode, Left Behind Alerts, and an IP67 dust- and water-resistant rating.

Though the Galaxy SmartTag 3 is compatible with iOS devices, the features available to Apple fans are limited, with Ring Phone, Left Behind Alerts, and Compass View reserved for Galaxy users. Compass View is enabled by Bluetooth Channel Sounding, an upgraded Bluetooth distance-finding technology. Despite Samsung embracing a low-cost boost to device tracking, Channel Sounding is locked inside the Galaxy ecosystem, a blow to the technology’s intended purpose.

Also: 3 ways Bluetooth 7 upgrades your devices beyond lossless audio

Channel Sounding is also Google’s Pixel Tag and Motorola’s Moto Tag 2, but these manufacturers open the technology to all compatible Android phones. However, Samsung’s SmartTag 3 doesn’t rely on Android’s vast but fragmented Find My Device network; instead, Samsung’s take on Channel Sounding will rely exclusively on the Galaxy Find Network. If a semi-closed ecosystem can help make evolving Bluetooth tech more reliable, does it matter that its implementation is counterproductive?

Samsung is the Goldilocks of device ecosystems. It’s not considered a walled garden like Apple, but it’s not as open to full third-party interoperability as Google. Many of Samsung’s most useful features are reserved for use within its Galaxy ecosystem. However, Samsung’s OS is built on top of Android, allowing for more flexibility than iOS, but still offering OS-exclusive features and, more importantly, feature reliability.

Full access to Samsung’s Galaxy Find Network is exclusive to Galaxy devices, similar to how full access to Apple’s Find My tracking features is reserved for Apple devices. On the other hand, Google’s Find Hub can accommodate Android phones from several manufacturers, including Samsung.

Also: Android is getting my favorite iOS tracking feature – what to expect

According to a press release, nearly 900 million Galaxy devices exist on the Galaxy Find Network. Each one’s constant Bluetooth signals contribute to an expansive network of crowdsourced data, extending the Galaxy FindTag 3’s reach and surfacing location data faster.

Google’s Find Hub’s greatest benefit is its scale: it can work with headphones, earbuds, Bluetooth trackers, smartphones, and smartwatches from multiple manufacturers.

However, different ecosystems limit tracking features to basic functionality, showing only where a device was last seen before it was powered off, or emitting a chime if you lose it. Live location data and accurate direction and distance finding from your smartphone aren’t possible.

Also: Apple has a Bluetooth problem, and Android is taking advantage

Implementing Bluetooth Channel Sounding aims to break down ecosystem-specific barriers, especially in a device-tracking context. If your smartphone, headphones, and smartwatch all support Channel Sounding, you could access fine-ranging tracking on all of them, regardless of device manufacturer.

Despite Samsung’s ecosystem providing it a device-tracking advantage, it defeats the purpose of Bluetooth: democratization. Basic Bluetooth connectivity allows any Bluetooth-compatible device to connect to another; that’s why you can wirelessly pair a pair of AirPods with a Lenovo laptop.

Also: Google’s Pixel Tag tracker has a big advantage over AirTags

Channel Sounding’s goal is no different in that it aims to bring more accurate distance awareness to Bluetooth-enabled devices, allowing you to finely track a pair of Sony headphones with an iPhone — that’s the goal, but not yet reality.

Samsung instead adopted Channel Sounding for its first consumer-ready endpoint within the boundaries of its ecosystem. Only Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, Galaxy Z Fold 8, Galaxy S26 Ultra, and Galaxy S26 Plus users can unlock the Galaxy SmartTag 3’s Channel Sounding capabilities when engaging its Compass View feature.

Also: Beware of Bluetooth sniffers: How your favorite gadgets could be exposing your data

All of these phones support Bluetooth 6.0 and Channel Sounding, but the Galaxy SmartTag 3’s Channel Sounding abilities will only be available to them and future Galaxy phones with Channel Sounding.

Conversely, Google’s Pixel Tag offers Channel Sounding to all Android phones that support it, including Galaxy phones. The result is that the Galaxy SmartTag 3 will operate just like any other Bluetooth tracker when paired with a base-model flagship phone, an older Galaxy phone, or an iPhone.

During this year’s WWDC, Apple announced Channel Sounding support for iPhones with its N1 networking chip and third-party Bluetooth 6.3 devices. Bluetooth 6.3 devices aren’t on the market yet and won’t be for a few years.

I assume Apple’s announcement of faraway future support is to give itself time to decide how Channel Sounding will fit into its walled garden, similar to Samsung’s implementation in the Galaxy SmartTag 3.

Also: How to tell if a hidden AirTag is tracking you – and disable it ASAP

Sure, Google’s Find Hub still needs some maturing; just last year, Google boosted the opt-in opportunities to add more devices for crowdsourced data, Find People is coming to Wear OS, and Find Hub is getting “Notify when left behind” alerts soon.

Apple’s and Samsung’s device location networks may be more feature-rich thanks to their closed ecosystems, but Google is working toward a truly open, easy-to-use network of devices powered by Channel Sounding. Which one is more important to you is for you to decide when it’s time to make a purchase.

#3147. Your November Stargazing Calendar: Meteors, Morning Planets and a Supermoon

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Darker evenings after the end of daylight saving time, plus a crowded morning sky, give you plenty of chances to look up this month.

Looking to see some amazing sights in the autumn sky? You’re in luck. November is the final full month of fall, and with daylight saving time having ended on Nov. 1, the sun has been setting even earlier. That’s good news, since some of November’s best views come before sunrise.

Venus, Mercury, Mars and Jupiter all appear in the morning sky this month, with Mars and Jupiter drawing close together around Nov. 15–16. The Leonid meteor shower peaks a couple of nights later, and the hours after moonset on Nov. 17–18 offer the darkest window to catch it. Evenings have their own highlights, from Saturn after dusk to the Beaver Supermoon on Nov. 24.

Below, find some of the remaining sights you should catch in the night sky throughout the rest of November.

Every planet is visible during the month of November, though depending on the time and day, you’ll get a better or worse view of them. Mercury and Venus are the most difficult to see due to their proximity to the sun.

Mercury: Mercury was at its eastern elongation during October, so it starts November a bit too close to the sun to see safely. It reaches western elongation on Nov. 20, when it’ll be easily visible just before sunrise for the rest of the month.

Venus: Venus starts the month just ahead of the sun at sunrise, technically making it possible to see every morning in November. It gets further from the sun as the month goes on, making it easier and safer to see toward the end of the month.

Mars: Mars is high in the sky all month. It rises out of the eastern horizon shortly after midnight at the start of November and rises earlier as the month progresses. Early morning is the best time to see it, or right around midnight toward the end of the month.

Jupiter: Jupiter and Mars are close pals for all of November, rising at roughly the same time and right next to each other in the sky. The star Regulus joins in to form a trio, which is visible to the naked eye the entire month.

Saturn: Saturn is also visible every night in November. It’s in the eastern sky when the sun sets, and sets on the western horizon shortly before sunrise. Right after dark is the best time to see it, but you’ll need binoculars or a telescope to capture its glorious rings.

Neptune: Neptune and Saturn are teamed up for November, with both of them being very close in the sky and following a similar trajectory. Bring binoculars or a telescope.

Uranus: Uranus is in the night sky every day in November, rising in the east shortly before sunset and setting in the west right around sunrise. It reaches opposition on Nov. 25, which means it’s as far away from the sun as it can get, and will be the most visible. You’ll still want to bring some binoculars or a telescope for best results.

Most of the planets are visible in the night sky almost every night in November, but on Saturday, there’ll be a fun little planet parade. It’ll take place just before sunrise, so it’s mostly for early risers. Mercury, Venus, Mars and Jupiter are set to line up nicely, making them easy to spot. This is especially true for Jupiter and Mars, which should be right next to each other that night.

The show will start around Saturday and will last until around Nov. 25, depending on your location. The tricky part is catching Mercury in the sky before the sun comes up. It’s only about a 30-minute window since the sun closely follows Mercury up over the eastern horizon. The single best day to view it is Nov. 20, when Mercury is at its western elongation — as far from the sun as it can get.

Uranus is also visible at this time, bringing the number of visible planets to three. Saturn and Neptune are below the horizon. Uranus is on the other side of the sky, however, so it’s not technically part of the alignment.

If you miss the Southern Taurids, you only have to wait a week to catch a glimpse of the Northern Taurids meteor shower. This is another long-lasting meteor shower that started on Oct. 20 and runs until Dec. 10. It peaks on Wednesday and Thursday morning. The American Meteor Society notes that the moon is only 5% illuminated on Wednesday, giving viewers even better conditions than during the Southern Taurids.

It is otherwise virtually identical to the Southern Taurids. The shower appears to originate from the same constellation, Taurus, which rises and sets at almost exactly the same times as it did a week earlier. The Northern Taurids promise about five meteors per hour under optimal conditions, with an increased chance of fireballs. Both showers are even fueled by the same comet, 2P/Encke. It’s the space equivalent of a sitcom rerun airing just one week later.

Leonids is usually the most active meteor shower in November. It started on Nov. 6 and runs until Nov. 30, making it shorter than both Taurids meteor showers. It peaks on the evening of Nov. 16 and the morning of Nov. 17.

The good news is that the meteor shower is very easy to find. Meteors from it will appear to originate from the Leo constellation, which is right next to Mars and Jupiter, which are visible in the night sky.

The bad news is that this part of the sky doesn’t rise until around midnight, making this a meteor shower for night owls. It should produce about 15 meteors per hour under optimal conditions, though you can expect slightly fewer because the 41% illuminated moon will create enough natural light pollution to obscure fainter meteors.

The Leonids have produced exceptional meteor storms in the past, with hundreds of meteors per hour. That isn’t expected to happen in 2026, but the odds aren’t zero. They may improve after the comet loops around the sun again in 2031.

A micro moon is noticeably smaller and less bright than a supermoon or even a regular full moon.

November’s Beaver Moon takes place just two days before Thanksgiving. It is also the first of a string of four consecutive supermoons that will close out 2026 and begin 2027. This happens when the moon is within 90% of perigee — its closest point to Earth. The phenomenon makes the moon appear about 7% larger than a regular moon and 14% larger than a minimoon — and noticeably brighter than both.

Per The Old Farmer’s Almanac, the Beaver Moon reaches its peak illumination on Nov. 24 at 9:53 a.m. ET, which is after sunrise for most people in the US. That means the best time to see it is either the night before (Nov. 23) or the evening after (Nov. 24). The moon remains over 90% full from Nov. 22-27. If you plan on going skygazing, avoid those days like the plague, since the moon creates a ton of light pollution.

It’s not often that the same event happens twice in a single month, but it turns out Jupiter, Mars and the moon just can’t seem to get enough of each other. The trio closes out the month the same way it started: hanging out very close together in the night sky. And yes, Regulus will once again tag along.

Unlike the prior meetup, this one only lasts for one night before the moon dashes away. Since all four of them are visible with the naked eye and the moon is still mostly full, people shouldn’t have any trouble finding them. Eagle-eyed stargazers may see Algieba nearby as well. It’s the second brightest star in the Leo constellation (behind Regulus), and it’s also visible without binoculars or a telescope.

The constellations continue their summer-to-winter shakeup. Prominent constellations in the sky include Taurus, Pegasus, Capricornus, Aquila, Pisces and Aries. Mainstays such as the Big Dipper and Little Dipper are still out there, but can be difficult to see if you live too far south. As a rule, we recommend using a sky map or a tool such as Stellarium to pinpoint each object.

There are also some lesser-known asterisms to seek out, such as the Pleiades (the Seven Sisters), the Great Square of Pegasus and the Circlet of Pisces. The Summer Triangle is still visible, while the Winter Triangle becomes much easier to spot as it rises above the horizon earlier in the evening.

#3146. Top Wall Street analysts suggest these 3 dividend stocks for steady income

The ongoing earnings season, investor concerns about the durability of AI demand and spending, and geopolitical risks are key factors that have been contributing to stock market volatility in recent trading sessions.

In this scenario, investors seeking steady income can consider adding dividend stocks to their portfolios. Recommendations of top Wall Street analysts can help them pick attractive dividend stocks that are backed by solid cash flows to support consistent payments.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Oil and gas exploration and production company ConocoPhillips is this week's first dividend pick. With a dividend of 84 cents per share (annualized dividend of $3.36 per share), COP offers a dividend yield of 3%. The company is scheduled to announce its second-quarter results on Aug. 6.

Ahead of second-quarter results, Wells Fargo analyst Sam Margolin reiterated a buy rating on COP stock with a price target of $183. Despite the pressure on oil prices from an increase in OPEC production quota, the analyst finds ConocoPhillips and Shell stocks appealing as the earnings season approaches. He cited their operational visibility and resilience as factors backing their appeal.

The 5-star analyst expects ConocoPhillips to meet its production guidance of 2.2 million barrels of oil equivalent per day at the mid-point. He expects lower Waha natural gas prices in the Permian Basin to be offset by stronger Brent crude premiums. Margolin expects capital expenditure to remain within COP's prior guided range of $12.2 billion annualized, with no significant impact on spending on the Northfield East project in Qatar despite the Strait of Hormuz disruption.

Overall, Margolin expects COP to generate about $3.5 billion in free cash flow (before working capital) and earnings per share of $2.94. He expects continued strength in COP's free cash flow and regular dividend growth through the completion of the Willow project in 2028/2029. Prior to the Willow project coming online, the analyst expects free cash flow to grow by about $2 billion in 2027 and 2028, assuming Brent crude averages around $60 per barrel.

"COP's track record of capital efficiency and strong Permian well productivity underpins its ability to pursue long-cycle developments," said Margolin.

Margolin ranks No. 457 among more than 12,300 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 70% of the time, delivering an average return of 13.3%. See ConocoPhillips Financials on TipRanks.

Energy Transfer is a limited partnership that operates 140,000 miles of pipeline and associated energy infrastructure. With a quarterly cash distribution of 33.75 cents per common unit ($1.35 per unit on an annualized basis), ET offers a yield of 6.8%.

Heading into Energy Transfer's Q2 earnings on Aug. 4, Jefferies analyst Julien Dumoulin-Smith reaffirmed a buy rating on ET stock with a price target of $23. The analyst noted that his adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization estimate of $4.46 billion is 1% below the Street's consensus of $4.49 billion.

The 5-star analyst noted that Energy Transfer has slightly outperformed Enterprise Products Partners recently. However, it still trades at a relative discount of 19% compared to EPD, which is below its historical discount range of 17%-20%. Smith believes that ET stock could be re-rated higher if the company provides a clearer long-term strategy for natural gas growth.

Furthermore, Smith expects the current energy market to support a stronger outlook for natural gas liquids and crude oil. "The current energy macro backdrop positions ET to benefit in all three commodities," said the analyst.

He expects Energy Transfer's adjusted EBITDA to grow at a 4.8% compound annual growth rate in 2027-2030, which is 1%-3% above Wall Street's expectations. In fact, Smith sees the possibility of additional upside if ET announces more natural gas projects. He added that investors will await details on final investment decisions on new natural gas projects and any clues about additional projects in the pipeline. The analyst noted that ET has announced new gas projects consistently in recent quarters.

Smith ranks No. 550 among more than 12,300 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 64% of the time, delivering an average return of 10.4%. See Energy Transfer Statistics on TipRanks.

Finally, let's look at energy giant Chevron, which is scheduled to announce its second-quarter results on July 31. Last month, the company paid a quarterly dividend of $1.78 per share. At an annualized dividend of $7.12, CVX offers a dividend yield of 3.92%.

Ahead of Q2 earnings, Jefferies analyst Lloyd Byrne reiterated a buy rating on Chevron stock and lowered his price target to $216 from $236. Byrne expects the company to report adjusted EPS of about $5.86 per share, nearly 9% above the Street's expectations.

The 5-star analyst highlighted that the challenges seen in Chevron's upstream business in the first quarter due to the disruption at the Tengizchevroil joint venture in Kazakhstan, Storm Fern downtime, and the Middle East conflict have largely been resolved. Consequently, Byrne expects production to recover in the second quarter to about 4,033 mboepd. He expects the upstream business to generate adjusted earnings of about $8.1 billion in Q2 2026.

Meanwhile, Byrne expects Chevron to generate downstream adjusted earnings of about $4.4 billion in Q2, with strength in both domestic and international markets. The downstream business benefited from higher crack spreads and strong refining performance.

Additionally, the analyst expects Chevron to generate $18.2 billion in cash flow from operations (before working capital changes), driven by stronger earnings and about $2.2 billion in dividends from affiliated companies. Unlike the first quarter, Chevron is not expected to make a TCO loan repayment in Q2, providing an additional boost to cash flow.

Byrne ranks No. 409 among more than 12,300 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 56% of the time, delivering an average return of 17.5%. See Chevron Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

#3145. Precipio (PRPO) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Precipio targets a $40 million run rate by 2027 as it expands its sales team.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Precipio, Inc. (PRPO +6.53%) reported third-quarter results characterized by a transition from achieving financial independence in 2025 toward a strategy of accelerated revenue growth for 2027. Management reported that the company achieved a quarterly cash balance exceeding $3.5 million while maintaining positive adjusted EBITDA and operating cash flow. The company stated its intent to leverage established distribution agreements with four major industry partners to scale its product division, targeting a combined annualized revenue run rate of $40 million by the end of 2027. This growth plan includes doubling the sales force and hiring a senior marketing executive to enhance clinical credibility and market awareness. Management noted that current facility infrastructure is already equipped to handle up to $100 million in annual revenue without further major capital expenditures.

Operator: Welcome to Precipio Q3 2026 Shareholder Update Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] Please note that the conference is being recorded. Statements made during this call contain forward-looking statements about our business. You should not place undue reliance on forward-looking statements as these statements are based upon our current expectations, forecasts and assumptions and are subject to significant risks and uncertainties. These statements may be identified by words such as may, will, should, could, expect, intend, plan, anticipate, believe, estimate, predict, potential, forecast, continue or the negative of these terms or other words or terms of similar meaning.

Risks and uncertainties that could cause our actual results to differ materially from those set forth in any forward-looking statements include, but are not limited to, the matters listed under Risk Factors in our annual report on Form 10-K for the year ended December 31, 2025, which is on file with the Securities and Exchange Commission as well as other risks detailed in our subsequent filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission. These reports are available at www.sec.gov.

Statements and information, including forward-looking statements, speak only to the date they are provided, unless an earlier date is indicated, and we do not undertake any obligation to publicly update any statements or information, including forward-looking statements, whether as a result of new information, future events or otherwise, except as required by law. Now let me hand the call over to Ilan Danieli, Precipio's CEO. Please go ahead.

Ilan Danieli: Good afternoon, everyone, and thank you for joining us. Before we jump into a review of the results for Q3 2026 and share several thoughts for 2027, I thought that as we come to the end of another successful year, it might be helpful to add another member of the management team to these calls. I'd like to introduce my Co-Founder and Precipio's Chief Operating Officer, Zaki Sabet. Along with Dr. Ayman Mohamed, the 3 of us started Precipio in 2011, and we've been inseparable since. Prior to founding Precipio, Zaki spent his career in the diagnostics industry. While at college, Zaki worked as an accessioner during the night shift in a lab in New Jersey.

And over the years, he moved up through the ranks of lab tech then supervisor to eventually manage the entire laboratory. Bringing his in-depth expertise, Zaki was responsible for building what is today, to the best of our knowledge, at our size, one of the few profitable hematopathology laboratories in the country. At Precipio, Zaki oversees all company operations, including both our clinical laboratory as well as operations for the products division, including manufacturing and supply chain. Today, Zaki will be joining me in sharing some remarks, and then we'll also be available to answer questions during the Q&A section.

As this is our last scheduled shareholder call of 2026, I'd like to put these results in the context of the progress we've made over the past couple of years and explain how that progress sets the stage for 2027. In 2025, our focus was on getting the company to a cash flow positive position. We've gone through several dilutive financings and decided that it was time for the company to stand on its own 2 feet and become financially independent. So we set our eyes on reaching cash flow positive through a combination of revenue growth alongside significant operational efficiency improvements. And at the end of 2025, we were there.

Our company was cash flow positive, no longer dependent on outside capital in order to survive. And for the first time, we were able to respond to the calls from the various investment banks and hedge funds looking to provide capital to Precipio with a polite but clear, no thank you. I can tell you, as the person responsible for raising money to keep the lights on for 15 years, that was a wonderful moment. The second goal in 2025 was to determine if the products we created and that were used in our own lab would be real value to other laboratories.

We carefully explored this market by identifying target customers in several segments, which would serve as an indicator of market interest. This meant reaching a better understanding of which products in which configuration suited each segment. It meant continuously refining our sales presentation and value proposition to give the customer what they wanted and also to determine which level of support was required by each customer.

While many investors have observed that our revenue in 2025 remained relatively flat, our learning experience was a critical step at that time and serves as an important foundation for us to determine the course for our sales team to efficiently target the market, for our R&D team to build the right products and for our support team to be well equipped to onboard our customers. At the end of 2025, we had accomplished 2 key tasks: first, financial independence; and second, a market understanding of our customers and our value proposition.

In 2026, with a better understanding of our customer base, our product mix and how we can best serve our customer, we set out to validate our go-to-market strategy, reaching customers via distribution. One of the things we learned in 2025 and before was that in the laboratory space, getting in front of the customer and meeting the right decision-makers is really difficult. And post-COVID, if you didn't have a personal relationship, it was near impossible. We also learned that once we were in front of the decision-maker, we were quite successful in making the sale. So how do we get that door open for us? The distributors hold an important role in this field.

Working with the top 4 distributors in the industry, Thermo Fisher, Medline, McKesson and Cardinal Health, we have learned the power of the 200-plus sales reps each of the distributors employ. These are armies of well-trained, experienced and well-connected reps that have a long-established relationship with their customer, often spanning 10 to 15 years. There is no amount of money that would enable us to replicate even a fraction of that sales force power. And so we decided that distribution was the way to go. We also learned that each distributor is different, with different organizational structures, divisional responsibilities between different reps and organizational culture differences that dictate how best to interact with each distributor.

In 2026, we set out to figure the recipe for success with each distributor. During this process, we also learned what were the internal skill sets we needed to develop within our commercial team to best apply each recipe with each distributor. As we stand now at the end of 2026, we feel we figured out most of what we set out to discover in terms of the recipe with each distributor. That has led to some new hires in our commercial team and to a clear internal articulation of our go-to-market strategy via distribution. You've seen the gradual growth of the product division over the first 3 quarters of this year.

While it's always nice to see the business grow, this is by no means satisfactory to us nor it is a reflection of our planned growth trajectory going forward, quite the contrary. Precipio will -- 2027 will mark an important next phase in Precipio's evolution as we shift our focus from developing and validating our commercial strategy to accelerated growth. With the right products, a clear understanding of our target customers and established distribution strategy and the commercial infrastructure we're putting in place, we believe we now have the foundation to pursue a significantly higher rate of growth in our products business.

For the first time, we'd like to share with shareholders some specific financial objectives against which we intend to measure our progress. For our product division, we are targeting an annual revenue run rate exceeding $10 million by the end of 2027 compared with approximately $4 million annualized run rate based on our third quarter results of 2026. Our pathology business will also remain an important part of our growth strategy. Beyond its role in supporting product development and clinical validation, it also continues to generate the majority of our operating cash flow. We intend to continue growing this business, targeting an annualized revenue run rate of approximately $30 million by the end of 2027.

Together, these objectives represent a combined annualized revenue run rate exceeding $40 million by the end of 2027. To be clear, these are targets for the annualized revenue run rate we aim to achieve as we exit 2027 rather than a forecast of total revenue recognized during the year. We believe achieving these objectives would represent a significant milestone for Precipio, demonstrating the scalability of our products business while strengthening the financial foundation that enables us to fund continuing growth, product innovation and expansion into new diagnostic markets.

We recognize that these are ambitious objectives and delivering against them will require disciplined execution, but we believe the progress made over the past 2 years positions us well for this next phase of growth. Now let's turn to a review of Q3. Total revenue increased from approximately $7 million in Q2 to $7.3 million in Q3. Pathology revenue was approximately $6.3 million and product revenue exceeded, for the first time, $1 million a quarter, an exciting milestone. Adjusted EBITDA was approximately $400,000, consistent with Q2. Our operating cash flow was approximately $600,000 compared with approximately $700,000 in the second quarter.

Total cash increased by approximately $0.5 million during Q3, bringing our quarter end cash balance above $3.5 million compared with approximately $2.3 million a year earlier. These results give us a stronger financial foundation. With the confidence of a consistently cash-flowing business, it's now time to shift the balance. While maintaining positive cash flow, we plan to shift our focus to significant accelerated revenue growth. So let's discuss how we plan to scale up for growth on the product side. 2026 is all about understanding the recipe for growth.

As we discussed, we view distribution as the key source of scalability for our products business, and we wanted to understand how to best make that channel work before committing resources to a broader commercial expansion. We deliberately approached this with a relatively small commercial team and a measured level of spending. We wanted to refine the distributor model and our overall sales strategy before building a larger sales and marketing effort around them. The sequence was intentional: establish the approach, learn from execution and then invest in scaling it. We now believe we have a much clearer understanding of that recipe and how to support it.

Our ability to connect effectively with the distributor reps, arm them with information to get us a meeting and proceed to build a pipeline, all give us confidence we're ready for the next stage. It's now time to shift our emphasis from developing the model and understanding the recipe to implementing and expanding its reach. In 2027, growth will be our central commercial priority. We intend to significantly expand the commercial team and set aggressive goals for them while increasing marketing and technical support behind our products. It's time to pour gas on the fire, utilizing the incoming cash flow as resources towards accelerating the distributor and sales approach we spent this year developing.

An important part of that plan is bringing in a senior marketing executive to lead initiatives that were not previously pursued at this level. We want a more active presence in the market and a more systemic way to build awareness, credibility and access to prospective customers. That includes a stronger presence at relevant conferences, where we can engage laboratories, clinicians and our distribution partners. It also includes building a network of key opinion leaders who can provide clinical insights and help inform the evidence needed to support adoption. We plan to build clinical credibility through additional publications and case studies that explain the application and value of our technologies.

Our products need to be supported with evidence useful to the physicians and laboratories making testing decisions. Marketing will also work closely with sales on prospecting and customer access. The goal is to identify the right accounts, reach the people involved in testing decisions and give our sales team stronger materials and more opportunities to substantive customer discussions. That should extend to our distributors as well as to our direct commercial efforts. These initiatives are intended to work together. Conferences create opportunities for engagements, clinical relationships and evidence, strengthen our credibility and coordinated marketing and sales follow-up help move that interest towards evaluation and adoption.

Since quarter end, we have made changes to the commercial leadership and are bringing our products and pathology sales efforts under a more coordinated structure. Our recent product training week brought commercial, clinical and operational teams together to deepen product knowledge and strengthen customer conversations. These steps all support the broader growth effort we are preparing for next year. We will measure progress through customers completing implementation, beginning clinical use and placing repeat orders, ultimately resulting in revenue growth. Aggressive goals need to translate into results, and we intend to maintain that discipline and focus as we expand our commercial activity.

As we move from developing our commercial strategy to executing against a much more ambitious growth plan, operational leadership and accountability across the entire organization will become increasingly important. Zaki has been instrumental in building the infrastructure that brought us to this point. So now I've asked him to join this call and share his perspective on how we plan to scale the business from here. Zaki, all yours.

Ahmed Sabet: Thank you, Ilan, and good afternoon, everyone. As Ilan has outlined, we've spent the last several years building the foundation for Precipio's next stage of growth. My focus has been on developing an organization that not only can deliver high-quality diagnostic services and products, but to do so efficiently, profitably and at a significantly greater scale than where we operate today. I believe one of Precipio's greatest strengths is the operational infrastructure we've already built, and the opportunity we now have to leverage that infrastructure as the business grows. Within our pathology division, we've demonstrated our ability to grow revenue while improving efficiency and profitability.

We've invested in our people, systems, processes and laboratory capabilities, creating an operating model that we believe can support substantial additional volume without requiring a corresponding increase in our cost base. On the product side, we applied that same philosophy. We've built manufacturing capabilities, quality systems and technical support infrastructure designed not just for our current level of sales, but for the much larger business we intend to build. And importantly, these 2 divisions are deeply connected. Our clinical laboratory is not simply a source of revenue and cash flow.

It is also where we develop, validate and continuously improve our technologies, giving us a unique understanding of how our products perform in real-world clinical environments, and what our customers need to implement them successfully. To put the scale of the opportunity into perspective, we estimate that our existing operational infrastructure has the capacity to support approximately $100 million in annual revenue, roughly equally divided between pathology services and product manufacturing without requiring significant additional capital investment in our core facilities and equipment. That is a substantial amount of capacity relative to where our business stands today, and it creates an important opportunity for us to scale revenue, improve margins and drive greater profitability as we grow.

Ilan Danieli: Thank you, Zaki. In summary, the progression is clear. In 2025, we focused on reaching positive cash flow and financial independence. In 2026, as we generated cash, we studied and refined the commercial approach we believed can scale our products business. In 2027, we intend to put significant resources directly towards implementing that commercial approach and focus entirely on growth. We enter the next year with a strong financial foundation and a clear commercial direction. Our task is now to turn that preparation into faster growth. I'd like to thank our dedicated team of employees for their work and to our shareholders for your continued support. 2027 is going to be another pivotal year for us.

Zaki and I will now take your questions. Thank you.

Sean Westropp: All right. Great. Good quarter. I wanted to ask a little bit about the product sales and the scalability. You talked a lot about it in your comments here. Part of it is also to meet the demand from our distributors as we strengthen our connections with them, we'll get more motivated, more and more prospects, more and more meetings that we need to handle.

Sean Westropp: Got it. Great. And then on that sales cycle and sales side, do you have any idea now that you've kind of got 4 in place around ramp-up time of these new folks? When do they start kind of ramping up to actually able to deliver some product sales?
