Sean Westropp: Right, right. Great. And yes, on the gross margin side, the product gross margin, no changes there. I don't think you guys have always had pretty healthy gross margins on that. Is there anything on the distributor impacts that would affect the gross margin or anything like that?

Ilan Danieli: No, no, not at all. That's baked into calculation. So we're currently hovering around the kind of high 40s, 50% gross margin. As we scale up, when we double our revenue, I think -- I'm trying to do the math in my head, but I think the margins jump to probably the mid-60s and we'll continue that way. So if we look at this quarter, we grew by $100,000, right? That's nothing.

#3144. Android Auto requires Android 11 or higher now – check your compatibility

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Mobile OS > Android

Android Auto's minimum requirements have changed. Here's what to know.

Google has officially phased out support for Android 9 and Android 10 for wired Android Auto use — so you’ll need Android 11 at a minimum to connect an Android phone to a compatible car via USB, according to an update to Google’s Android Auto support page spotted by Android Authority. Android 11 through Android 17, the most up-to-date version, are fully supported for Android Auto (though Android 17’s adoption rate remains quite low).

These changes confirm early reports that Android 10 users saw warnings that their devices would soon lose Android Auto support, even before Google’s documentation had specified the change.

Also: Got an old car? Android Auto is easy to add: 2 ways, starting at $20

It’s not uncommon for Google to drop the oldest Android versions that can still run Android Auto every few years. In 2024, Android 8, released in 2017, was dumped from service. Android 11 was first released in 2020.

Android Auto brings apps to your car display so that drivers can focus better on the road. It allows you to control features such as navigation, maps, calls, text messages, and music, and is the Android equivalent of Apple CarPlay.

Also: 5 Android Auto apps that make my life easier on the road

The requirements have changed little since last year, aside from the new minimum software requirement. The new instructions for wired Android Auto support are straightforward: Phones must be running Android 11 (Red Velvet Cake) or newer, have an active data plan, and be supported by a compatible car. Google also recommends a quality USB cable.

Android Auto is integrated into compatible phones, so you do not need to download it. Android Auto isn’t available on devices that run Android (Go edition).

Also: I was a big wireless Android Auto fan, until I tried wired – now I won’t go back

To find out if your car or stereo is compatible with Android Auto, Google has a hub page to help. For more information about your car’s compatibility with Android Auto on your car display, it’s best to contact your vehicle manufacturer.

For drivers still using older phones running Android 9 or Android 10, getting Android Auto back will require either replacing a current device with one that runs Android 11 or newer, or installing an available software update on a current device.

Also: Gemini on Android Auto can access my photos, emails, and calendar – why I’m OK with that (mostly)

#3143. Apple TV Adds Sign Language Interpretation, Starting With Original Film ‘Being Heumann’

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Tech > Services & Software > Streaming Services

It's the latest streaming service to add American and British Sign Language options, making movies more accessible and enjoyable for a wider audience.

Apple TV is adding sign language interpretation for a handful of supported streaming titles, beginning with the Apple original film Being Heumann, which premieres on Friday.

With iOS 27.2, you’ll find new options for American Sign Language and British Sign Language within Apple TV’s app settings. When you select one of these languages, a new button will appear on supported Apple original titles indicating sign language availability. You can also turn off or change your language selection directly within the player.

Titles that support sign language interpretation will have a sign language icon displaying an image of a hand. This icon appears on the title page of a show or movie, next to other accessibility options like closed captions and audio descriptions.

Being Heumann is an apt pick for debuting this accessibility feature. The film centers on the true story of disability rights activist Judy Heumann (Ruth Madeley) and her leadership in the historic 1977 protest that helped advance equal rights and protections for Americans with disabilities. Sign language support will also roll out to other Apple TV titles starting with F1 The Movie, followed by Greyhound and Way of the Warrior Kid (which debuts Nov. 25) later this year.

Apple TV is adding a dedicated collection called Movies & Shows with American Sign Language to make it easier to browse supported content. That collection will include movies where sign language is part of the story, such as 2021’s Oscar-winning film CODA. You can also look up “with ASL” in the app’s search bar to find relevant titles.

“We believe everyone should be able to enjoy great stories and entertainment,” Sarah Herrlinger, Apple’s senior director of Global Accessibility Policy and Initiatives, said in a statement. “Bringing sign language interpretation to Apple TV is an exciting step forward in making the viewing experience more accessible and inclusive for Deaf audiences.”

Apple TV joins a handful of other streaming platforms with sign language options, including HBO Max and Prime Video. Netflix also features sign language interpretation for dozens of kids and family titles through a partnership with SignUp Media, which built a Chrome extension that overlays an interpreter onto supported shows and movies. SignUp is also available on select Disney Plus and Peacock content.

While closed captioning can help some deaf and hard-of-hearing people better understand what’s happening on screen, many viewers prefer watching with sign language interpretation, which can better convey emotion and expression.

“For the deaf community, our first language is ASL,” Nakia Smith, a deaf storyteller and an interpreter for the HBO Max series It: Welcome to Derry, told me in an interview earlier this year.

Unlike closed captioning, which has become nearly ubiquitous across streaming and television, sign languages like ASL are slowly making their way into more entertainment spaces, from sports broadcasts to awards ceremonies and red carpets. But there’s still a long way to go.

The challenge is that sign language interpretation requires skilled human professionals who can capture context and nuances, which takes time and resources. More companies appear to be making the effort. And while some studios are exploring AI to automate captioning, the complexity and diversity of sign languages suggest this will remain a largely human-driven endeavor for the foreseeable future.

For its part, Apple worked closely with the deaf community, partnering with Directors of Artistic Sign Language to ensure they matched the tone of the films and maintained authentic representation.

“It’s incredibly meaningful to see our beautiful language authentically represented onscreen,” Daniel Durant, who appears in Being Heumann and who directed the film’s sign language interpretation, said in a statement. “Bringing this experience to life required a lot of care to ensure every translation captured the emotion and meaning of the story. I’m proud to have been part of Being Heumann and thrilled to see Apple TV supporting greater accessibility for Deaf audiences.”

#3142. Google Pixel Tag Hands-On: The AirTag for Android Fans

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Google’s own tracker adds a few welcome details to the smart tracker field.

When a company comes out with its own version of a product in an established market, there has to be a good reason. Maybe it’s created a design that sets the product apart, or it’s included features that none of the competition has.

If you think I’m talking about Apple and Google, you’d be right – but this isn’t the iPhone Duo muscling into the folding phone fray. This time, the roles are reversed: Google is releasing the Pixel Tag, a small Bluetooth tracker that it hopes will be the Android ecosystem’s answer to Apple’s near-ubiquitous AirTag.

The Pixel Tag is available starting Wednesday for $30 each or $100 in a pack of four. It works with Android phones and uses Google’s Find Hub technology for tracking over distances beyond Bluetooth range. If you use an Android phone and have wanted the capability to track things such as keys, bags, bikes, vehicles and other indispensable items, and you want the tech to come from the company that designed the system, the Pixel Tag is an excellent choice.

It isn’t the first Android-compatible tracker. Motorola introduced its Moto Tag 2 earlier this year, and Tile has been the de facto AirTag alternative for several years. There’s also now a growing ecosystem of other items that tap into Apple’s Find My and Android’s Find Hub networks, ranging from slim credit-card-sized devices like the Rolling Square AirCard Pro and Peak Design’s Beacon Finder Card, to novel approaches like Falcam’s TagBatt, a battery for some Sony and Canon mirrorless cameras that integrates Apple Find My tracking.

Google jumping into this more crowded field tells me the company thinks there’s profit to be made by manufacturing its own hardware and software. It’s also investing in the infrastructure it’s already built out, and not leaving the hardware side to a constellation of other vendors.

Trackers like the Pixel Tag and AirTag can be a surprisingly deflating purchase: You pair them with your phone, put them into something you don’t want to lose track of – then forget about them. They’re usually not tactile the way a phone, watch or laptop is each day. And their value doesn’t kick into action until you think an item has gone missing.

After slinging AirTags into bags and dangling them off keychains, one thing I really appreciate about the Pixel Tag is its thinness. Apple chose a small, round footprint, even keeping the exact design for the second-generation AirTags. Google instead opted for a longer lozenge shape, at 1.8 inches (46.1mm), that is about two-thirds the height of the AirTag at 0.2 inch (5.4mm).

Google sent a Bellroy leather keychain as a sample accessory for review, and paired with the Pixel Tag, the two are a fine size for a pocket or clipped to an inside bag pocket. I thought the longer design would get in the way, but it’s not bad at all.

The Pixel Tag uses a CR2032 coin-sized battery that should last about a year (the same as the AirTag). It also has an IP67 rating, which is durable in 1 meter of water for up to 30 minutes.

Another departure from the AirTag is a physical button, making the Pixel Tag even more tactile. When you’re using Find Hub on your phone to locate it by sound, press once to stop the chirps it makes. Or, if you have the tag in hand (on a keychain, for example) and need to find your phone, press twice to ring the phone – it makes a pleasant sing-songy chime that gets louder and more intense as it continues, so I’m confident it’ll be easy to locate, even among couch cushions.

Speaking of the chimes, credit to the Google sound designers who came up with the Pixel Tag’s tune. It has three levels of loudness you can set, and seems plenty audible enough when you’re spelunking the living room for it. I measured it at 80 decibels, which when compared to the second-generation AirTag volume, is 7 less than the 87 decibels of Apple’s tracker.

One more nice touch compared to the AirTag: the Find Hub app shows the tag’s battery status. If that gets to Low or Very Low, the app sends you notifications every two weeks until the battery is replaced. After Apple showed battery statuses on AirTags in early versions of the Find My app, the company changed the Find My app so it only indicates battery when it’s low and needs to be replaced.

The best feature of either tracker is the ability to locate its exact location – not which building or room it’s in, but to tell if the item fell behind the couch or was accidentally dropped in the driveway. (Yes, I’m making up these examples from personal experience.)

Precision Finding uses a combination of Bluetooth 6.0 (via a feature called Channel Sounding) and the ultra-wideband chips inside the tag and the phone to directionally find the tracker when it’s within Bluetooth range. You hold the phone upright, perpendicular to the ground for the best connection. Then you wander your space, watching the indicator change as you get closer to the tag.

On the Pixel Tag, that indication is a wobbly circle shape that fills in as you get closer; when you’re on top of the tracker, the shape is fully filled. The Find Hub app also uses the camera and UWB chip to include an estimated distance in feet and inches (or meters and centimeters). When you’re close enough, the tracking shape becomes a directional arrow to point you the right way. UWB is compatible with the Pixel 8 Pro, Pixel 8 Fold and newer Pixel phones.

In my testing, the Find Nearby feature performed fairly well. Find Hub using a Pixel 11 Pro XL connected from within about 25 feet, including on multiple levels of a house when I was above or below it.

Perhaps because I was raised on science-fiction devices like the trackers in Aliens, though, I expected more consistent readings. There were times when both I and the tag remained stationary. The distance estimates would fluctuate by several feet.

Since I’ve had this review unit for only a couple of days, I haven’t yet had a chance to send it off with someone else and see if I can track it remotely using the Find Hub network. When nearby Android devices detect the Pixel Tag’s presence, they should securely and privately relay the tracker’s location to Google’s servers. (Apple’s Find My network operates the same way.) I’ll update this article once I’ve taken the tag on such an adventure.

Tracking all your stuff is invaluable – I learned this first-hand earlier this year when I left a small bag containing my passport in a hotel room, and was able to convince the hotel that the bag was still on the premises. But unfortunately, smart tags are being used to track people without their knowledge.

Google is taking the same approach as Apple to help thwart this type of tracking. If a tag is separated from the phone it’s paired with (or the phone of someone else you’ve chosen to share the tag location with), and the tag is moved, its chime activates.

The idea is that you’ll hear an unfamiliar chirp and investigate. It has an NFC chip that displays its information when you tap it using the NFC built into a phone.

#3141. Ready for a Siri AI agent? Apple under pressure to upgrade its assistant faster

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Home & Office > Smart Home > Smart Assistants

Apple's public-facing satisfaction with the Siri AI launch obscures internal pressures and tensions.

Apple’s recently appointed CEO, John Ternus, is allegedly pushing the company internally to ramp up its AI strategy — including making Siri an AI agent.

Also: My 5 favorite Siri AI ‘onscreen awareness’ tricks

According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, the CEO is publicly pleased with the Siri AI launch, but privately encouraging Craig Federighi, Apple’s SVP of software engineering, to move faster.

“Desiring more and frustrated by what he sees as a reluctance to embrace AI with the same urgency as competitors, Ternus pushed his software chief to accelerate the company’s road map and move quickly beyond merely making necessary improvements to Siri,” Gurman wrote. He added that the tension stems from Federighi’s reputation as an AI skeptic.

The revamped Siri AI is now a much better voice assistant with some helpful features. Gurman noted he thinks Siri AI’s ability to automatically fix your weak passwords is already somewhat agentic behavior, though AI-generated passwords have their own issues.

But Siri AI isn’t yet on par with increasingly autonomous agents from AI-first companies that aim to proactively organize your tasks, use your computer, and write advanced code. Still, those rival agents deliver a patchwork of capabilities: while some, like OpenClaw and Anthropic’s Claude Code, are highly functional, others, like Google’s Gemini Spark, aren’t quite there yet.

Also: I tried replacing Claude Code with a free local AI stack

Regardless, the issue here is time. Despite developing powerful hardware perfectly suited for running local AI models, Apple has remained slower than competitors on the AI software front. Competitors have demonstrated they can make promised agent features a reality, some quicker than others.

On the other hand, the fact that Apple hyped Siri AI for two years only to release an improved voice assistant (rather than a groundbreaking AI product) may mean users are ready for more advanced features.

In addition, AI companies are working on their own hardware. “If they can combine that software with AI-native devices designed from the ground up around assistants that see, remember and act, Apple’s longstanding advantages could begin to matter less,” Gurman wrote.

An agentic Siri would most likely build on what users already like about the new version.

The on-screen awareness feature, for example, is currently limited to what’s visible on your screen in that moment, meaning only the part of a long email that you’ve actively scrolled to. An agentic Siri could ideally scroll all the way through an email on its own and surface the insights you’re looking for.

Also: The iPhone made Apple a giant – but the Mac could help it win the AI era

But in the short term, Ternus’ push will likely just deliver on existing promises. Gurman also pointed out that Siri AI still lacks advanced in-app actions, which Apple initially announced in 2024 and would let third-party apps create plug-ins for and pathways through Siri.

“This functionality would let Siri tap into both in-house and third-party applications with more precision,” Gurman wrote. “This past week, as part of the first beta version of iOS 27.3, Apple finally began talking about the feature again.”

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, ZDNET’s parent company, filed an April 2025 lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

Plus, if we’re talking about agents specifically, newcomers like OpenAI’s Dot and Anthropic’s Duet aren’t competitive themselves yet: ZDNET’s AI vetter-in-residence David Gewirtz found both to be “a little odd” and not “quite ready for prime time”.

Also: I tested OpenAI Dot and Anthropic Duet for weeks – and all I got was one helpful notification

For users who appreciate the subtlety of Siri AI, though, anything similar to ChatGPT or Claude on their devices might not land, unless each feature is opt-in.

#3139. Can Cathie Wood's Ark Invest ETF Make a Comeback With Its Large SpaceX Position?

SpaceX will make the Ark Innovation ETF more volatile, and AI trends ultimately determine the fund's fate.

Discussions about Cathie Wood being a better investor than Warren Buffett feel like a distant memory. Still, her flagship Ark Innovation ETF (ARKK -2.38%) has produced an annualized 15.5% return over the past decade. However, that also includes an annualized 9.1% loss over the past five years, showing the volatile nature of the fund.

Consistent with high volatility, she has quickly turned Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX +0.72%) into her second-largest holding, behind only Tesla (TSLA +0.46%). Elon Musk has a big say in how Wood's fund performs, but is that the right move? Here's what investors should consider.

Ark Invest CEO Cathie Wood. Image source: Getty Images.

You won't find the slightest bit of value investing in Wood's portfolio, unless you count Nvidia (NVDA -5.47%) as a value stock. While that's a fair argument due to its relatively low P/E ratio, it's hard to call companies like Coinbase (COIN -2.92%), Tempus AI (TEM -4.62%), and OpenAI value stocks. These three companies make up the fund's top 10 holdings, and they are extremely volatile.

Consistent with its annualized five- and 10-year returns, investors can expect a volatile ride with dramatic price action. SpaceX fits the mold, with many 10% upswings and downswings since its June IPO.

A 0.75% expense ratio certainly works against the fund's desirability, but it is well positioned for the most high-risk, high-reward AI opportunities.

A $1.8 trillion market cap implies a lofty valuation and may limit future growth opportunities compared to smaller AI stocks. However, the business is undeniably growing at a rapid pace. Revenue surged by 161% year over year, with net operating income of $2.8 billion as a major highlight.

The super intelligence segment is doing the heavy lifting. That part of the business grew by 830% year over year to $7.56 billion. Growth almost tripled sequentially. Space revenue was also up 84% sequentially, showing that it's not just an AI data center stock. For now, though, AI is still firmly in the driver's seat of SpaceX's future growth.

The primary concern is whether most of future growth is already priced in at a $1.8 trillion market cap. However, SpaceX's earnings results and Musk's desire to have up to 20 gigawatts of power by the end of 2027 suggest that more gains are possible. Granted, Musk will have to achieve that 20-gigawatt total, which may be more difficult due to midterm election results.

Ark Innovation holders should watch closely for any AI developments. The tone of the industry will directly impact Wood's fund in a meaningful way since it is heavily exposed to the industry. However, a 0.75% expense ratio is a bit too high for me.

AMD has admitted a bug within its External Events Utility is wearing out SSDs, and promises a fix.

Under normal circumstances, an SSD might go all day without needing to access or write files. But for some AMD Radeon users, anything but normal circumstances are causing drives to continuously write and re-write data. The External Events Utility (EEU) that AMD installs alongside its CPU and GPU drivers is reportedly the culprit.

Also: Nvidia RTX 50 GPUs hit with more price hikes

Fortunately, there are a few workarounds available to avert disaster while AMD works on a more permanent solution.

Reports of the issue first surfaced in July on AMD’s official PC user forum, with one user stating that the External Events Client Module and EEU were constantly writing information to their SSD after installing a Radeon 9060XT graphics card. Subsequent comments on the thread this month confirm that the issue has persisted despite several bug fixes and patch updates, with two users reporting hard numbers for data usage ranging from 0.3 MB/s to as much as 1.5 MB/s.

Also: The best laptops: Expert tested and reviewed

This week, Reddit user darklinkpower posted that the AMD Adrenaline Edition desktop application also had the EEU driver bug, using up to 1% of their drive health per month for around 16 months. That might not sound like much, but it can cause catastrophic problems if left unchecked.

AMD seems to be aware of the issue; a company official who goes by AMD_Vik on Reddit commented that it will “hopefully [be] fixed in the next [update].” While there’s little indication of how quickly a permanent, official patch will be pushed to users, there are a few ways you can protect yourself from the bug and prevent your storage drive from collapsing.

This seems to be the most consistent fix for most AMD users reporting issues, but disabling the EEU can cause its own problems, such as disabling AMD FreeSync support or introducing display glitches if you hot-swap screens while your PC is powered on.

The AMD Adrenalin Edition desktop app lets you control how your PC components communicate with one another, and it might be another facet of a complex problem. By allowing your CPU to access your graphics card’s memory, you can temporarily boost performance, but the EEU bug seems to let it and your GPU run rampant, eating up every bit of memory they can find. Changing a few settings within the app may help:

Also: I tried local AI on HP’s Omnibook Ultra

This is a more niche solution that carries its own risk of introducing communication issues between your CPU and GPU, so I only recommend trying this route if disabling the EEU itself doesn’t resolve the issue. AMD’s official fix may be in the works, but without a firm timeline for release, users are left twisting in the wind trying to stop their PCs from hemorrhaging storage capacity.

Automatic network switching for Pixel phones could mean fewer mobile dead zones.

Even in areas that seem abundant with overlapping cellular coverage, phones sometimes sputter when you’re looking up information or trying to get directions when your carrier’s signal gets weak. To avoid those annoying interruptions, Google Fi Wireless is rolling out what it’s calling a “super network” feature. It automatically switches your phone between two 5G networks to maintain the best connection.

The new capability works only on Google’s phones, starting with the Pixel 9 and newer Pixel models.

The super network is included free for existing Google Fi customers on all of its plans: Flexible, Unlimited Essentials, Unlimited Standard and Unlimited Premium.

Google says that it’s using “two top 5G networks,” but the company is refusing to reveal which networks those are in the US. Traditionally Google Fi runs on T-Mobile’s network.

The network switching also applies when you’re traveling internationally, and is included in the Unlimited Premium and Flexible plans.

According to a source at Google, the phone will use two eSIM slots to switch between networks, but it will appear to only use a single eSIM on the customer’s phone. A fine-print disclaimer notes that any other eSIMs on your device must be disabled, which is worth knowing for anyone that already uses multiple carriers on a single device.

In addition to the super network news, Google said its Wi-Fi Auto Connect Plus feature is available in millions of more locations across the US. If the phone is in an area where cellular is spotty and a compatible Wi-Fi network is nearby, it automatically makes an encrypted connection if the Wi-Fi network is stronger.

Wi-Fi Auto Connect Plus is available on Pixel phones, but is also becoming available on Samsung phones running One UI 9 or later and “select modern Motorola phones.”

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Windows > Windows 11

The latest Windows 11 Insiders Preview enhances the Search feature so that you can access specific settings right from a search window.

Microsoft has been on a kick lately trying to improve and enhance Windows 11, including sprucing up Search, which is now simpler, cleaner, and friendlier. And there’s another cool trick that Search has up its sleeve: Available in the Beta channel of the latest Windows 11 Insiders Preview, Search will give you access to specific Windows settings and commands. Known as inline actions, this latest skill is designed to help you directly complete certain tasks. That means you no longer need to know exactly where or how to find the setting you need.

Also: Windows 11 can run better on PCs with 8GB now

Curious about built-in features such as Dark mode, Bluetooth, screen brightness, Remote Desktop, the Windows clipboard, or Windows Update? Just type the name or phrase in the Search field. The results then display an Open button that you can select to go directly to the related setting.

“A new Windows Search experience built on WinUI 3 is beginning to roll out,” Microsoft said on a web page announcing the latest Insiders build. “It’s faster, more efficient, and features a streamlined design that makes results easier to scan. Inline actions let you quickly complete tasks directly. Turn on dark mode or Bluetooth, adjust your screen brightness, mute your device, or arrange windows from Windows Search.”

I tried this with several different Windows settings, and the results window pointed me to the right screens for tweaking them. Though I know where most Windows settings are located by now, there are still times when I forget how to reach certain ones. Also: 11 Windows apps I replace on every new PC

With the latest update, Search will now better understand what you actually mean and match you with the correct results. Type “drak” instead of “dark,” for example, and you’ll still see the results for Dark mode.

Microsoft promises these latest improvements to Windows Search will continue to be fine-tuned over the next few weeks. And there’s more in the new Preview build.

Ever run into trouble using Windows Hello facial recognition in a dark area? Now, your screen will temporarily brighten up to help you sign in under those conditions. To enable this option, head to Settings, select Account, select Sign-in options, and then click Facial recognition. Turn on the switch for “Automatically adjust screen brightness during face recognition.”

The latest Insiders build also tweaks features such as Live captions, Gaming, File Explorer, and Microsoft 365 cloud storage.

Also: How I used ChatGPT to talk me through fixing a corrupted gaming PC

To grab this update, you’ll have to join the Windows Insiders Program if you’re not already registered. You can then sign up for the Beta or Experimental channel, either of which will give you access to the new Search skills and other features. Make sure you’re running the Beta Preview Build 26320.9876 or higher. To check, go to Settings, select System, and then click About. The Windows Info section will indicate the build number.

As for regular Windows users not enrolled in the Insiders Program, the new changes should reach you relatively soon. I’d expect them to roll out with the December Patch Tuesday update arriving on December 8, so that Microsoft can squeeze them in before the end of the year.

#3133. Why the S&P 500 Could Be Heading for a Repeat of 2018

Back in 2018, President Trump was in power, and the Republicans lost control of Congress after disappointing midterm results, just as they have recently.

If the S&P 500 (^GSPC -0.38%) is able to stay above a 10% gain for the year, it'll be the fourth consecutive year that it has been able to produce above-average returns. It's a rare feat. But it's not common for a reason, as sooner or later, there's inevitably a pullback.

The last time the market crashed was in 2022, when the broad index fell by more than 19%, due to rising interest rates. Over the broad part of the past five years, however, it's been fairly resilient.

But I do see similarities between now and 2018, which could be cause for concern. That was during President Trump's first term in office, and midterm elections also took place that year. And, just like now, Republicans would end up losing control of Congress. While 2018 wasn't as bad as 2022, the S&P 500 did fall sharply in the last two months of the year.

There have been many articles discussing how the S&P 500 typically rises after the midterms. And while that's correct, there is a glaring exception to that, which is 2018. Unfortunately, there are also multiple parallels between then and now, including both who the U.S. president is and what happened during the midterms. Back in 2018, Republicans still held on to a majority in the Senate, but Democrats would obtain control of the House of Representatives.

Following the results, the stock market went into a tailspin. Between November and Christmas that year, the S&P 500 declined an incredible 14%. The index would recoup some gains after Christmas, as it would shrink its losses to about 8.5% between November and the end of the year.

Whether or not 2026 ends up being a repeat of 2018 or not, there are plenty of reasons to be extra cautious these days. Not only are valuations for many stocks incredibly high, but interest rates may rise again before the end of the year, inflation remains problematic, and although the overall economy is still doing well, there are many people who are struggling as consumer sentiment has been declining.

For investors who want to minimize risk, a good option may be to consider investing in exchange-traded funds (ETFs) that focus on stable sectors of the economy, such as utilities. The Vanguard Utilities ETF offers exposure to utility stocks while also paying a relatively high dividend that's currently yielding 2.8%.

Investors, however, have many ways to diversify beyond just tracking the S&P 500, and now may be a critical time to do so.

#3131. Can you still trust Proton?

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

The company’s reputation took a major hit two weeks ago, when 404 Media published a detailed report, based on leaked Slack messages and interviews with anonymous insiders. The story detailed a push by Proton CEO Andy Yen to — in his own words — “ruthlessly smash everything that stands in the way of AI velocity.”

Also: Is your browser’s free VPN enough? I tested 4 against Proton VPN

After one employee proposed spending at least a few days on penetration testing before shipping new code, Yen reportedly said, “That’s bullshit and loser thinking. Of course it’s possible to be fast and secure. Stop thinking always of how to be slower, and focus more on how to be faster.” According to 404 Media’s account, Yen’s message for Proton engineers was to “stop lovingly handcrafting all our code and use AI more.”

After the original story broke, 404 Media posted a follow-up story reporting that the company had canceled its “re-interviews” that were intended to assess how developers were adopting AI. A 404 Media podcast was titled “Proton’s CEO Is Putting AI Before Security.”

Reddit has an especially active Proton community with 345,000 weekly visitors. It quickly filled up with so many comments — the majority of them negative — that moderators created a single megathread to help keep track of the different threads, including pages for general criticism, support of the AI usage, and “leaving your goodbyes.”

Also: Best VPN services 2026: Expert tested and recommended

Given the level of interest, it’s not surprising that Yen chose that forum to post a public message to the community. In it, he apologized for “hurtful” remarks, adding that he’s “determined to do better.”

He also addressed the topic of AI-based security reviews:

But most importantly, I need to categorically state that our use of AI will never be at the expense of security. In the past year, contrary to what has been alleged, actually additional layers of security review have been added to meet the threat posed by hostile AIs scanning Proton’s open source code for vulnerabilities. Fast and secure need not be mutually exclusive. We also leverage AI to find vulnerabilities in our own code before attackers do. Our code is open source, and its security remains open for all to verify. [emphasis in original]

Nothing in the 404 Media reporting demonstrates that Proton weakened its encryption or shipped insecure code because of AI. The damage is different: Yen’s remarks undermined confidence that management will consistently respect the security processes its customers rely on.

In a blog post that Proton shared with ZDNET ahead of its publication today, the company followed up on Yen’s promise to “lift the hood on how we use AI internally at Proton.” The post, titled “How Proton keeps your data secure in the age of AI,” was signed by the Proton Team and emphasizes Proton’s secure architecture, with end-to-end, zero-access encryption:

We do not hold the keys to your emails, files, or passwords, so we cannot read them, and no AI tool can, either. Our documented security governance policies have not changed since June 2024, before AI was even a major factor in our work here, and they all still apply.

On Reddit, Yen said, “AI is here, and it will unquestionably change how software is developed forever, and Proton must also change.” Today’s post clarified that code receives the same checks whether it is written by a human, by an AI agent, or by a combination of both. Every change receives automated security scans but also requires human approval; sensitive changes, such as core cryptography work, require review by specialist teams. Major feature designs are also reviewed for security, dependencies, testing, and deployment plans.

Also: I can access my home PCs remotely for free – no VPN needed

Those policies address the most serious technical concerns raised by the current controversy, although outsiders have no way to know from the policy alone how consistently those safeguards are followed in day-to-day development.

Should a modern software company use AI for security? Proton argues that it can’t afford not to.

Because of AI, attacks that once might have required a nation-state can now be executed by almost anyone. A defender relying on manual processes and hand-crafted tools is bringing a knife to a gunfight. An attacker only needs to find one flaw, while a defender needs to close all of them. AI is the only tool that makes that defense possible. Cybersecurity is an arms race, and the teams working on security at Proton have been some of the earliest adopters of AI, because the safety of your data depends on winning that race.

But that argument doesn’t really address the objection. The current controversy isn’t about whether Proton should use AI to find vulnerabilities; it’s about whether pressure for “AI velocity” can override the judgment of engineers responsible for keeping its products secure.

Proton says it uses AI to review code changes, identify vulnerabilities through continuous security reviews, and monitor an attack surface that has “grown far beyond what unaided humans could monitor.” The company uses its own models alongside non-public cyber models from OpenAI and Anthropic.

The modern software development landscape is torn by two opposing forces. On one side, you have AI-based tools that are routinely finding nightmarish vulnerabilities in existing codebases and then exploiting them immediately. On the other side, you have a global movement that’s skeptical of the benefits of AI and outright opposed to construction of the data centers where they run.

Much of Proton’s growth over the past few years has been the direct result of people trying to escape big tech. So it shouldn’t be a surprise that many of Proton’s customers — at least those who are passionate enough to visit a Reddit forum — are deeply skeptical of anything related to AI.

Also: Ring’s new drone patrols your home to keep an eye on things – even upstairs

In a traditional software company, that realization would have led management to cautiously roll out AI-based features and reveal its AI-centric security strategy more deliberately. That didn’t happen here, obviously. Those blunt remarks from the CEO exposed a management culture that many employees and customers found troubling. It’s difficult to restore trust, both within the workforce and among customers, after that kind of public display of contempt.

Ironically, one of Yen’s comments from the original 404 Media story describes the company’s current dilemma with devastating accuracy.

In a Slack message, Yen told a Proton engineer, “perception is more important than truth, the truth doesn’t matter if you don’t win on perception.” The implication was that he was urging the employee to lie, or at least shade the truth. In fact, as Yen himself told a random Reddit commenter:

I do not believe perception should be more important than truth. I am stating that unfortunately it often ends up being the case. If you place it into the context in which it was said, it can be understood as, “it doesn’t matter that the truth is that Proton’s PQC implementation is better, this truth is irrelevant as long as it is not perceived to be this way, and we therefore need to correct that perception”

That’s Proton’s challenge now, distilled to its essence. It takes seconds to destroy a reputation. It can take months or years to recover from the perception that the company and its management can no longer be trusted.

Personally, I will continue to use Proton Pass and Proton VPN, both of which are solid, reliable products. But I’ve moved my secondary email accounts (which I had migrated from Gmail to Proton Mail); they’re now running on Fastmail. I had been considering making the switch for a long time, primarily because Proton Mail’s performance has been too slow for my taste. Current events just hastened that switch.

#3128. Neoclouds Like Nebius Are Much Better Investments Than Colocation Companies Like TeraWulf. Here's Why.

Neoclouds are a much better long-term opportunity than colocation providers.

Hyperscalers need gigawatts of energy to fuel their artificial intelligence ambitions, and there are two key categories of service providers that every investor should know. Neoclouds like Nebius (NBIS -5.27%) are the first option, while colocation companies like TeraWulf (WULF +1.45%) are an alternative.

The common narrative is that neoclouds are riskier investments but also have a higher ceiling. Neoclouds have more expenses since they also buy AI chips, whereas colocation providers like TeraWulf require tenants to bring their own chips. That business model results in lower capital expenditures and makes it easier for colocation providers to build facilities.

When you take a closer look, the neocloud formula is far more promising than the colocation model. Here's why.

Let's start with recent deals Nebius and TeraWulf have secured. While Nebius offered flashy press releases about long-term contracts with Microsoft (MSFT -2.21%) and Meta Platforms (META +0.00%) in the past, it has been a bit more discreet about customers.

Nebius told investors in its Q2 shareholder letter that it's getting long-term deals at $20 million to $25 million per megawatt. That matters because some hyperscalers require hundreds of megawatts for a small slice of their AI needs. One hundred megawatts at $20 million per megawatt equals $2 billion in annual recurring revenue. Nebius is aiming for a 5-gigawatt pipeline by the end of the year. Short-term deals are being signed at $40 million to $50 million per megawatt.

TeraWulf's big deal was a 20-year, $19 billion contract with Anthropic for 401 megawatts. That comes to about $2.4 million per megawatt per year. TeraWulf has lower costs since it's not responsible for AI chips, but that's a 20-year deal where TeraWulf cannot capitalize on rising megawatt prices. It's locked into a low-megawatt rate for a long stretch, and if the costs of building and maintaining AI data centers continue to rise, it could squeeze TeraWulf's margins.

Some bearish analysts have pointed to high capital expenditures that AI data center providers must pay to build facilities and buy chips. Nebius has higher costs, but financing and lucrative deals have mostly solved this problem.

Nebius told investors in its Q2 shareholder letter that 50% to 60% of its capital expenditures are financed by prepayments. The company can also borrow against its GPUs, knowing it can secure competitive rates and profit on those chips as more contracts materialize.

The company's payback period has quickly dropped from two to three years to just one year and 10 months. As megawatts get more expensive, the payback period could drop even further. That's how long it takes for Nebius to generate enough revenue from deals to cover the costs associated with building and maintaining data centers and buying chips.

Once those payback periods are reached, Nebius can start funding its data centers with incoming profits instead of borrowing money. If Nebius continues to borrow capital, it will have an easier time finding competitive rates as it becomes more profitable.

TeraWulf does not have this advantage. It can't charge $20 million to $50 million per megawatt because it doesn't have the chips. Even after TeraWulf completes its payback period, it doesn't have the full stack like Nebius.

As neoclouds like Nebius continue to sign lucrative deals and shorten payback periods, they will be in a better position than colocation providers like TeraWulf to accumulate more gigawatts.

Fellow neocloud Iren (IREN -7.85%) disclosed a 35-gigawatt development pipeline. That doesn't mean Iren will convert all 35 gigawatts into AI data centers, but colocation companies don't have the same scaling power to support that type of expansion.

It wouldn't be shocking if Nebius had a similar development pipeline. Even if Iren secures only 10 additional gigawatts out of the 35, it may be enough to turn Iren into a generational wealth opportunity. The same goes for Nebius.

Iren and Nebius aren't going to sign deals at $2.4 million per megawatt. In fact, Iren revealed a new long-term deal at $22 million per megawatt in its fiscal 2027 first quarter results. It's also getting short-term deals at $40 million per megawatt.

Artificial intelligence has already produced generational wealth for some investors. While the AI data center play is hot right now, there is a critical difference between a neocloud and a colocation provider. Neoclouds have much higher ceilings, and the few bearish points continue to be snuffed out with each earnings report.

#3126. How AI security failures are endangering your supply chain – and what you can do

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

New research provides a stark look at the AI supply chain and the risks it brings to businesses.

Artificial intelligence companies worldwide are bringing a new wave of vulnerabilities and security issues to the digital supply chain, researchers warn.

According to a new report published by Black Kite on Tuesday, there now exists a “widespread cybersecurity weakness” across the “rapidly expanding ecosystem of companies developing, deploying, and supporting artificial intelligence.”

AI and smart solutions don’t automatically equate with safe solutions. In a study titled “2026 AI Supply Chain Report: The Risks Behind Your AI Relationships,” Black Kite says that many AI suppliers — the companies that develop and deploy AI services to today’s businesses — are struggling with “basic security practices.”

Also: Rogue AI incidents hit ‘tens of thousands’: Can businesses trust these tools?

According to the research, after examining the companies themselves, along with their software, integrations, and components, researchers found failures to patch critical vulnerabilities, protect credentials, authenticate users and email, and address network security issues.

The study analyzes 18,160 AI companies worldwide, ranging from 0-10 employees to more than 1,000 employees. A company’s AI involvement was determined through reviews of company products and services and primary business activities, covering six broad groups: everyday application development; AI development and implementation; AI applications in specialized sectors such as healthcare, IT, and finance; industrial organizations; and AI foundations working on data, compute, and modeling.

A small percentage of assessed companies are considered “unclassified,” and the study excluded businesses that use AI only incidentally.

In addition, unusual network activity was detected at 44.3% of organizations, and botnet-related activity was recorded at 41.8% of AI companies.

AI’s main business appeal is its ability to integrate with existing software and platforms to handle manual tasks, heavy lifting, and tedious, time-consuming work, freeing employees to focus on work that requires human oversight.

Enterprises are investing billions of dollars in AI. Menlo’s 2026 research estimates that enterprise AI spend reached $37 billion in 2025, with half of overall spend going to AI apps. In total, 76% of enterprise AI solutions are purchased rather than built internally.

However, the moment an AI or automated component is introduced into a corporate ecosystem or operational platform, any security problems it has impact the user — and each additional integration, such as software components or open-source tooling, may also increase the attack surface.

In an accompanying analysis of AI firms’ use of Model Context Protocol (MCP) components, which can link AI apps to business systems, 48.8% of 1,732 logged security findings were rated High or Critical, including code and command injection vulnerabilities.

Also: The new enterprise AI expert every company needs

It’s not just the AI application itself. As noted by Black Kite, AI suppliers often have access to customer data, developer environments, business infrastructure, and enterprise platforms. If the supplier’s credentials are stolen, this could expose its customers to a range of cyberattacks.

The researchers found, for example, that 19.9% of AI companies offering solutions for enterprise AI deployment had corporate login information in infostealer records, and that stolen corporate logins, overall, were linked to 6.8% of AI suppliers in the study.

Visibility matters, too, for businesses that should be monitoring their digital supply chains. However, 33.2% of AI companies assessed have a “limited” digital footprint, including their domains, subdomains, and IP addresses.

The same principles for protecting the digital supply chain apply to AI suppliers, where continual monitoring and assessment are among the best protections businesses have.

Staying informed and aware of the risks to your own business makes all the difference. As recommended by Black Kite, it takes more than a single point-in-time security assessment — frequent monitoring and engaging with suppliers to understand their technologies and dependencies can reveal potential security issues.

Also: Do you need AI agent liability insurance?

If you find weaknesses, manage them by priority, handling ransomware-related exposures and vulnerabilities actively exploited in the wild first.

Also audit an AI tool’s integrations and components, access, what data it can reach, and the potential impact of exploitation. Once you’re armed with this information, it’s possible to weigh risk and reward — and whether the AI tool is worth the potential attack exposure it brings. If you decide to keep it, limit its permissions and access to what it requires.

Alongside the Ring Drone Cam, Ring introduced the Rover Cam for businesses. It investigates disturbances and streams 4K footage.

Today, Ring announced the launch of a new subbrand, Ring Robotics, with two new products: the $249 Ring Drone Cam, an indoor “mobile security camera” drone that shoots 2K video, and the $999 Ring Rover Cam, a security robot for businesses that patrols autonomously and investigates disturbances.

Also: Amazon’s new Echo Studio gives Alexa+ an AI camera to see inside your home

Both devices use Ring’s custom navigation software, “AI Pilot,” to autonomously navigate interior spaces and move between set points along a patrol, rather than being controlled directly by the user. AI Pilot leverages the devices’ cameras, sensors, and vision models, along with cloud processing, to create interior maps, then move the devices between predesignated patrol points such as a side door or a window.

I recently saw both new robots in person at a showcase in New York hosted by Ring’s founder and chief inventor, Jamie Siminoff. They certainly do what they advertise but come with some significant limitations. The drone, for example, can only stay in the air for about 8 minutes before it needs to dock and recharge, while the Ring Rover Cam is slow and deliberate, seemingly ideal for routine surveillance rather than rapid response to an event.

The Ring Drone Cam moves around predetermined patrol points in your home, sending you a live 2K video feed whether you’re just in another room or out of town. The user doesn’t actually fly the drone; instead, it moves around autonomously using Ring’s custom “AI Pilot” navigation technology, leveraging its cameras, sensors, and cloud processing to create a map of its surroundings. This allows it to fly through the air at an appropriate height, going from room to room, even up stairs.

In the Ring app, the user creates patrol points they want the drone to move between — likely a window, doorway, or high-traffic room — creating a set path that is both predictable (so you always know where the drone will go) and relevant, so it’s only monitoring the areas you want it to. But here is where its limitations come into play: It needs a finite path to navigate because its flight time is limited to just five to eight minutes in the air before it has to return to its charging dock.

That makes the dock both the start and end point for the drone’s routine trips, and it’s designed with this in mind. When it goes to land, the drone hovers over the dock and lowers itself down, dropping into place so it can start charging automatically. I asked about its potential to land elsewhere, and Ring told me it would only make an emergency landing outside of its dock in case it didn’t have enough power to get home.

Also: Amazon’s new Echo Dot can turn into a Wi-Fi extender – how it works

There’s one other very important caveat: This thing is loud. There’s no sneaking up on anyone with the Ring Drone Cam, as the entire household is likely to hear it the second it undocks. The four propellers emit a constant, high-pitched whirring while in the air that’s loud enough to announce its presence to anyone in the vicinity: intruder or resident.

During the product briefing, Siminoff insinuated that this was part of its design to dissuade home intruders snooping around your house at night (especially when paired with the drone’s front-facing spotlight), but it’s likely just the result of its engineering, especially considering this is a first-gen product. It’s so loud that it makes me think it’s better suited to navigating the home when no one’s home (although whether or not your pets go bonkers trying to catch it is a whole other issue).

The Ring Drone is designed to work out of the box with the existing Ring ecosystem, including the 2K Video Doorbell and Indoor Cam, and is also compatible with Amazon’s Map View.

The Ring Drone Cam will start shipping on Jan. 27, 2027, and will cost $249.

The other product Ring announced is the Rover Cam, a mobile robot with a 4K camera designed to monitor large spaces like warehouses, offices, or businesses. Ring calls it a “security guard that never clocks out,” but it’s more like a slow-moving droid that goes on set patrol paths. It leverages the same AI Pilot technology as the Ring Drone to map its surroundings and navigate around shelving, furniture, and obstacles in real time.

It’s much quieter than its airborne sibling, traveling at low speeds and offering mobile surveillance instead of wiring every square inch of a large space. If the technology here looks familiar, it’s because it resembles the Amazon Astra, a smaller robot designed for home monitoring but with a very similar build.

The idea here is to deploy the robot to certain areas of a workplace via the app, then get 360-degree views once it’s there. Like the drone, it can also set out on automated routes at select timing intervals — like right after a business closes or before it opens. During working hours, it chugs along with its camera, capturing everything in its view.

Also: The 4 biggest Amazon smart home announcements from today

If another Ring device is triggered, the Rover Cam autonomously goes to investigate the disturbance, providing 4K footage in real time via the app. It also features a periscope camera that can extend to see over obstacles like shelving, counters, or furniture, providing a high-level view if needed. In case you lose it in a large warehouse or office, it has a “light tower” that projects light upward onto the ceiling, notifying users of its location.

Even when docked, it uses motion-sensing technology to start recording the second it senses any kind of movement, just like Ring doorbell cameras. In case of an emergency, the Rover features a siren and red flashing lights to dissuade intruders.

The Ring Rover Cam is available for preorder now and will start shipping on Dec. 16, 2026. It will cost $999.

They prioritize driving performance over everything

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I’ve said it countless times this year: If there’s one type of vehicle I’ve driven more than anything else, it’s the 3-row family hauler. When you’re looking for maximum passenger capacity without skimping on comfort, full-size SUVs certainly fit the bill — and the Nissan Armada and Dodge Durango are no exception.

Unlike mainstream models like the Chevrolet Tahoe or GMC Yukon Denali that prioritize plush comfort over driving dynamics — often making them feel like lumbering giants — these two are far from it. Instead, these heavyweights prove that family practicality and raw enthusiasm can genuinely coexist.

The $55,225 as-tested 2026 Dodge Durango R/T 392 AWD Launch Edition delivers pure old-school muscle with a 475-hp 6.4-liter HEMI V8 engine that sounds genuinely imposing. That looks like a steal next to the $83,735 as-tested price of the 2026 Nissan Armada Nismo, but the Nismo counters with a twin-turbo V6 pushing 460 horsepower, sharper styling, and enough high-tech amenities to make a case for its steeper sticker.

After testing each one for a week, only one earns my recommendation.

2026 Dodge Durango R/T 392 AWD Launch Edition

NISMO-Tuned 3.5L Twin-Turbo V6 Engine (4WD)

17 mpg city / 16 mpg highway / 19 mpg combined

13 mpg city / 19 mpg highway / 15 mpg combined

Frankly, neither design captured my attention at first — but one of them eventually grew on me. Even though they compete in the full-size, 3-row segment, they take entirely different styling routes.

The 2026 Dodge Durango R/T 392 Launch Edition leans hard into classic muscle swagger — reminiscent of the Dodge Charger — with its scooped performance hood, functional air intakes, bold Brembo brake calipers, and a rounded profile that still looks surprisingly menacing. It catches plenty of glances thanks to that aggressive stance, but it lacks the visual flair to truly sell me on its familiar look.

Between the two, the 2026 Nissan Armada Nismo gets my nod. Despite its noticeably more upright, boxy proportions, it delivers far more drama and curb appeal. Nissan gave it the full NISMO treatment, outfitting the SUV with massive 22-inch machined alloy wheels, an aggressive front fascia and grille, sculpted side steps with flared fenders, and full-width LED taillights. The sharp two-tone premium paint finish seals the deal, transforming this traditionally square full-size SUV into an imposing showstopper worthy of a cameo in a Fast & Furious flick.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

2026 Dodge Durango R/T 392 AWD Launch Edition

Nobody shops for performance-tuned, three-row SUVs with the intent of saving on fuel. However, one of these gas-guzzlers still proved friendlier at the pump over the long haul.

The 2026 Dodge Durango R/T 392 Launch Edition surprised me most on dedicated highway runs, achieving a best mark of 24.2 mpg and handily overdelivering on its 19-mpg highway rating. On short-distance trips, I averaged 21.6 mpg — equally impressive given its 13-mpg city EPA estimate. Overall, it managed 18.1 mpg across 237.9 total miles of mixed driving.

In comparison, the 2026 Nissan Armada Nismo made a much stronger case for real-world consistency. While its best recorded long-distance run of 23.9 mpg fell just shy of the Dodge, its twin-turbo V6 and 9-speed automatic worked far more efficiently across everyday traffic. Over the course of 302 miles of mixed driving, the Armada Nismo delivered an average of 19.9 mpg — not only beating its official 17-mpg combined EPA rating, but also comfortably edging out the Durango by nearly two full miles per gallon overall. When you’re feeding a sport-tuned hauler week in and week out, that spread makes a noticeable difference.

When SUVs are slapped with performance badges, driving dynamics are what make them special over conventional haulers. While the Armada managed to surprise me in a big way, the Durango takes the crown here.

Nissan deserves immense credit for defying expectations given the Armada's boxy proportions, which initially made me apprehensive about driving it on crowded highways. It packs a genuinely strong 3.5-liter twin-turbo V6 pushing 460 horsepower and 516 lb-ft of torque, delivering instant thrust and effortless passing power.

It's also surprisingly easy to drive for its size, thanks to an ultra-responsive steering wheel that feels very light and loose. If that’s not enough, its adaptive electronic air suspension and great shocks make cruising over bumpy roads a breeze.

Yet for all the Armada’s composure, it can’t match the raw power and exhilarating feel of the 2026 Dodge Durango R/T 392 Launch Edition. Backed by a 475-horsepower 6.4-liter HEMI V8 under the hood, it completely transforms the driving experience.

Between the thunderous exhaust roar, immediate throttle response, and quick Brembo stopping power, the Durango delivers a far more thrilling ride every time I put the pedal to the metal. Honestly, it handles like a muscle car — giving enthusiasts the genuine excitement that almost every other three-row hauler lacks.

Both SUVs deliver great accommodations when it comes to passenger capacity, but one takes interior luxury and space to another level. What I love about both full-size haulers is how they offer second-row captain's chairs paired with a convenient center console for cupholders and armrest storage.

In the Dodge Durango R/T 392, second-row passengers have 38.6 inches of legroom to stretch out comfortably, while the third-row bench yields 33.5 inches. Even though adults can fit back there, my knees practically touch the seatbacks in front of me. Finally, there’s a cavernous 17.2 cubic feet of cargo space behind the third row that easily swallowed my electric scooter without needing to wedge it at an angle.

The one big downside for the Durango is that it lacks lane-centering assist when adaptive cruise control is engaged — meaning, it won't actively keep you centered between the lines.

The 2026 Nissan Armada Nismo simply offers more cabin volume to comfortably seat adults while pampering them with genuine luxury. Thanks to its taller cabin, legroom feels far more generous in the second row with 39.2 inches of space, while the third row provides 32.9 inches. The Armada also delivers significantly more cargo capacity behind the rear seats with 20.4 cubic feet of trunk space.

Between its plush, red-and-black trimmed NISMO suede seats, whisper-quiet cabin insulation, and ProPILOT Assist for hands-free highway cruising, the Armada makes long distance drices effortless no matter where you sit. That said, its lane centering isn't always spot-on when activated, but the overall luxury leap is impossible to ignore.

On paper, the pricing advantage leans heavily toward the Durango, but it's important to look at what each model actually delivers before jumping to conclusions.

Dodge’s value proposition is centered squarely on performance, yet this bargain full-size SUV still includes a respectable set of amenities. For example, you get a single-pane sunroof, a Harman Kardon sound system, and a standard backup camera. Still, I’m not as impressed with the dashboard layout, which leans far too conventional and dated.

By contrast, the 2026 Nissan Armada Nismo commands a steep $83,735 as-tested price that’s nearly $28,500 higher than its rival. That’s a significant stretch, but it buys a modern suite of luxury and tech features: an expansive panoramic moonroof, a high-fidelity 12-speaker Klipsch premium audio system, heated front seats, and a sophisticated 3D Enhanced Intelligent Around View Monitor that makes navigating tight parking spaces a breeze.

While the Armada undoubtedly delivers the more modern, tech-rich experience, the Durango's $55,225 as-tested price makes it an untouchable performance bargain in the three-row space.

I can’t overstate the price disparity between these two sport-tuned SUVs, with one costing nearly $28,500 more than the other. At their core, however, both deliver large family-hauling utility without forcing you to completely give up your passion for driving.

Without question, the 2026 Nissan Armada Nismo is the superior all-around modern SUV for everyday living. Between its sharp two-tone finish, plush suede seats, massive passenger volume, whisper-quiet cabin, and cutting-edge tech suite, it feels every bit like an $84,000 flagship that justifies its price tag. If your budget allows, the Armada won't disappoint with its effortless acceleration and smooth, composed ride — making it tough to beat.

2026 Dodge Durango R/T 392 AWD Launch Edition

Yet when it comes to the vehicle I’d actually spend my own money on, the 2026 Dodge Durango R/T 392 AWD Launch Edition gets my vote, despite coming up short on paper once all the category scores are tallied. Sure, the Durango's interior aesthetics lack the modern flair of its rival, but it unapologetically prioritizes genuine muscle car performance with three rows of seats.

With an as-tested price of $55,225, it isn’t just competitive — it's an untouchable performance bargain in a segment otherwise dominated by $60K+ land yachts.

#3120. Is the Stock Market Going to Crash? Warren Buffett's Warning Is Hard to Ignore.

Warren Buffett has invested through various economic cycles and understands how to navigate uncertainty and volatility.

Over the last several years, the S&P 500 (^GSPC -0.38%) generated total returns of 26%, 25%, and 18% in 2023, 2024, and 2025, respectively. Meanwhile, the Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC -0.74%) and Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI -0.30%) also delivered impressive gains.

Much of this rally has been fueled by artificial intelligence (AI) stocks. However, enthusiasm has spread beyond semiconductor companies and cloud computing providers to adjacent industries, including utilities, energy infrastructure, and data center construction.

While these trends have created enormous wealth, they also raise questions about stock market valuations. Between 1965 and 2025, Warren Buffett helped Berkshire Hathaway deliver a staggering cumulative return of 6,099,294%, compared with 46,061% for the S&P 500, including dividends!

Given that track record, Buffett's warnings about excessive speculation deserve attention. Right now, one of his favorite valuation metrics is flashing a concerning signal.

Warren Buffett. Image source: Getty Images.

In a 2001 interview with Fortune, Buffett introduced a valuation metric that subsequently became known as the Buffett indicator. The calculation divides the total market capitalization of publicly traded American companies by the country's annual economic output. Buffett originally used gross national product (GNP), although modern versions commonly substitute gross domestic product (GDP).

The higher the reading, the more expensive the stock market is relative to the underlying economy. Buffett once described this relationship as the single best measure of stock market valuations, warning that when the ratio approaches 200%, investors are "playing with fire."

As of this writing (Nov. 10), the Buffett indicator hovers around 228%, well above the threshold Buffett associated with speculative conditions. The broader message here is that stocks are expensive relative to economic output. This suggests investors are paying historically elevated prices for future earnings.

During Berkshire Hathaway's annual meeting in May 2026, Buffett compared financial markets to a "church with a casino attached." His point was that long-term investing and short-term speculation have become intertwined.

There's nothing inherently speculative about investing in AI companies with accelerating revenue and expanding earnings power. However, investors can still overpay for quality businesses.

When stock prices rise faster than underlying earnings, valuations expand. Eventually, companies must deliver enough profit growth to justify those premiums. Otherwise, even a minor disappointment can trigger massive selling pressure.

We are already seeing how quickly sentiment can change. During the first week of November, the Nasdaq declined roughly 3.4% while the S&P 500 fell 2.7%, as investors reassess AI infrastructure spending and its potential regulatory challenges. Although stocks have rebounded sharply, the volatility illustrates how sensitive investors can be when expectations change.

According to its latest quarterly filing, Berkshire held approximately $377.4 billion in cash and short-term Treasury bills as of Sept. 30. This gives the investment conglomerate extraordinary financial flexibility.

BRK.B Cash and Short Term Investments (Quarterly) data by YCharts

With that said, Berkshire isn't sitting completely idle. Under new CEO Greg Abel, Berkshire repurchased approximately $9.6 billion of its own shares during the third quarter and continued making selective investments.

In other words, Berkshire is willing to deploy capital when opportunities look attractive, but it isn't abandoning its liquidity cushion. I think retail investors can learn something from that approach. With valuations elevated and volatility reminding investors how quickly sentiment can reverse, maintaining some cash on hand could be wise.

Moreover, we're also approaching a period when year-end portfolio rebalancing, profit-taking, and tax-loss harvesting may contribute to outsize selling pressure. Of course, these activities don't necessarily cause broad market declines. A correction of 10% or more is certainly possible. A more severe bear market or crash can't be ruled out, either.

Of course, neither the Buffett indicator nor Berkshire's cash balance can reliably predict when those events will occur. For now, investors may want to consider reviewing concentrated positions, trimming holdings that have become disproportionately large, and maintaining enough cash to capitalize on attractive opportunities.

Remember, Buffett built his fortune by purchasing wonderful businesses at fair prices, not by attempting to predict every market downturn. The stock market may continue to climb, but elevated valuations suggest investors should be prepared for a meaningful pullback. If that happens, having cash on hand could turn a disorienting market decline into a compelling long-term buying opportunity.

#3119. 5 apps I need Siri AI to work with now that it’s open to third-party developers

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Home & Office > Smart Home > Smart Assistants

With the latest betas for iOS and other platforms, Siri AI is now available to all developers for full integration into their apps. Here are the ones I hope will jump on board.

One of the many benefits of the new Siri AI is its ability to work directly with apps on your device via a feature known as App Intents. Currently, this skill includes many of Apple’s own built-in apps and some third-party ones. But with the latest public and developer betas for iOS 27.3, the company is expanding support to all third-party developers.

Also: Ready for a Siri AI agent? Apple under pressure to upgrade

With App Intents, you’re able to ask Siri to tackle a variety of actions among various built-in and third-party apps. On a basic level, you can tell it to perform tasks such as getting directions, playing music, scheduling meetings, sending messages, adding reminders, and finding photos.

On a more advanced level, you can ask it to do things like organize your inbox, edit a photo, and analyze and help you with your current screen. You could also tell it to combine several actions in one shot, work across multiple apps, and engage in a natural back-and-forth conversation.

Introduced in 2022 with iOS 16, the App Intents skill does play well with classic Siri, no Apple Intelligence required. This applies not just to built-in apps but also to third-party apps. However, classic Siri lacks the AI smarts and advanced skills of the latest version.

Siri AI fully supports most built-in apps, including Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather. It does support some third-party apps, but its more advanced features are limited or unavailable.

That’s the gap the new developer betas aim to close. With iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, MacOS 27.3, and VisionOS 27.3, all developers will be able to use Siri AI to fully support and integrate with their apps. For example, instead of manually opening an app like DoorDash or Grubhub to check or change a food order, you can tell Siri to do it for you.

Also: The Siri AI waitlist is gone in iOS 27: How to try the beta now

“Today’s preview allows any app to bring its content and actions directly into Siri AI by using App Intents, making it easier for all apps to tap into Siri AI’s newest capabilities, including personal context understanding, on-screen awareness, natural language, and more,” Apple said in a news release for developers. “So people can just ask for help in their own words, and Siri AI carries out any custom action you’ve built, from checking a delivery to booking a reservation to placing an order.”

As I use many third-party apps on my iPhone and iPad, both personally and professionally, I’m looking forward to enhanced support for the ones I rely on. With that in mind, here are five apps for which I’d welcome the new and full Siri AI integration.

I often use Amazon on my iPhone and iPad to shop for and purchase items, review my wishlist, and check the status of products I’ve ordered. To do any of those things, I have to open the app and manually go to the right screens. How convenient it would be if I could tell Siri to handle those tasks for me.

“Siri, search for the 512GB 2026 iPad mini on Amazon and add it to my shopping cart.”

“Siri, review my Amazon wishlist for the luggage I recently added and tell me the latest prices.”

“Siri, check the delivery status of the Alexa photo frame I just ordered on Amazon.”

Right now, Siri can’t do any of those things. But if Siri AI and App intents are fully integrated with Amazon, I may just be able to accomplish those tasks in the future.

IMDB is my go-to app for getting info on movies, TV shows, performers, directors, and more. After I open the app and run a search, I often want specific details, such as the rating and runtime of a particular film or TV episode.

Also: AI completely changed how I develop iPhone apps

To simplify that process, I’ve love to be able to ask Siri: “Siri, search IMDB for the 1935 movie ‘The Bride of Frankenstein,’ give me the running time, tell me where I can stream it, and add it to my watchlist.” If Siri could accomplish all that at some point, it would get a round of applause from me.

I borrow and read a lot of e-books through my local library systems, and I use the handy Libby app for that. Here, I can search different libraries for books by title, author, or subject. I can then borrow a book and read it through the Libby app or, more typically, through the Amazon Kindle app. For this, I have to manually open the app and search among the various libraries for the book I want.

Also: I lost 100 pounds in 7 months: How a smart scale and Apple Watch helped

Instead, I’d like to ask Siri to do that for me. I might say: “Siri, look in Libby for books about Alan Turing, give me the titles of the ones you find, and tell me which ones are currently available to borrow.”

My wife and I are big theater buffs, and we see a lot of plays on Broadway when we’re in New York and on the West End when we’re in London. Often, I buy tickets through the TodayTix service and app. For this, I’ll open the app, set the location to New York or London, look for a specific play, and then try to find seats for a certain day and time.

If TodayTix is ever fully supported by Siri AI and App Intents, I might be able to ask Siri to track down the right seats for me. I could say: “Siri, look for the play ‘Rent’ in London, give me the available performances for Dec. 5 through 9, and let me know which seats are accessible in the first 10 rows.”

As my wife and I often travel and dine out, Yelp is another app I frequently use. Here, I also have to manually launch the app and run searches for restaurants and other places. I then have to try to filter or sort the results based on location, price, and ratings.

Also: 3 handy iPhone features that make my life easier – even doing laundry

Asking Siri to tackle those tasks would certainly be a time saver. I could ask it to “find the closest Italian restaurants using Yelp and show me ones within a one-mile radius that have earned four stars or higher.”

With App Intents, Siri AI can already handle advanced, complex, multi-step tasks for built-in apps. With all developers now able to take advantage of this same support, I’m expecting a lot of apps to jump on board. Let’s hope my favorites end up on the list.
