#3072. Is Nvidia a Bad-News Buy or a Stock to Avoid?

Nvidia has been a key winner in the AI boom.

Nvidia (NVDA -5.47%) stock has been one of the major winners of the artificial intelligence (AI) revolution. This is because the tech giant has built an AI empire, offering the world's fastest AI chips, known as graphics processing units (GPUs), and a full portfolio of supporting products and services. AI customers have snapped up Nvidia's chips, with demand often exceeding supply as the company launches new updates.

All of this has fueled mind-boggling earnings growth, with revenue and profit rising in the double and triple digits. Investors recognized this early in the AI boom, and this helped the stock soar 1,100% from the start of 2023 through the end of last year. This year has been a rockier one for Nvidia and other AI powerhouses as investors turned more cautious on the space. They worried about higher inflation in the U.S. and questioned whether data center spending would continue at current levels.

And just this week, particularly bad news concerning Nvidia emerged. Nvidia opened an investigation into chief Jensen Huang's relationship with a person U.S. intelligence agencies are calling a Chinese spy. Against this backdrop, is Nvidia a bad-news buy or a stock to avoid? Let's find out.

First, let's take a step back and consider Huang's role at Nvidia. He founded the company more than 30 years ago, and over time, he has been at the helm, guiding its direction. Huang made a major bet on AI about a decade ago, deciding to shift Nvidia's GPU focus to serving that market. Clearly, it was a winning decision. And since that time, he has become the face of AI development, speaking around the globe about the technology today and its future potential.

Huang also has lobbied to bring Nvidia's chips back to China after a U.S. export ban. He won that battle, with the U.S. permitting the export of certain chips, but China hasn't yet fully accepted imports. Nvidia has only exported a small number of chips there this year. But this situation brought the U.S./China AI race to the forefront.

All of this demonstrates something big: Huang is the driving force at Nvidia, a leader whose name is known around the world and well beyond tech circles. That suggests trouble for him could equal trouble for the company.

Now, let's consider the latest news. Nvidia on Nov. 8 said it is launching "an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort."

Huang, in an email to staff obtained by CNBC, said that he is "committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security."

The company also said in a statement to CNBC that Huang is committed to leading Nvidia "without interruption."

Nvidia's stock declined 4.2% in the following trading session, leaving the stock trading at 19x forward earnings estimates -- a level that's dirt cheap considering the company's track record of growth throughout the AI boom and prospects down the road.

Still, the current investigation introduces an element of uncertainty. So you may be wondering if you should pick up shares of Nvidia after this recent bad news or if you should avoid the stock.

The major risk the company faces is the possibility that Huang could step down or be forced out. Since he is a visionary who has driven the company for decades, and Nvidia hasn't set out a succession plan, investors could frown on such a scenario -- and that could weigh on stock performance. Another risk is that lawmakers might favor more limits regarding chip exports to China or increased regulation, moves that may weigh on future growth.

The decision to buy or avoid Nvidia right now depends on your comfort with risk. If you're a cautious investor, you might favor waiting for the results of the investigation before getting in on the stock. Though Huang intends to remain at the helm and the board has expressed confidence in him, uncertainty will linger until the investigation is complete. And this could hurt the stock in the near term. Any possible departure by Huang would also be bad news.

That said, the current turmoil doesn't change the demand present in the AI market or the quality of Nvidia's chips and innovation. Aggressive investors with a well-diversified portfolio might consider picking up a few shares of Nvidia at today's dirt cheap levels and holding on as the storm passes.

#3071. Greg Abel's Berkshire Hathaway Owns 37% of This Company. Here's Why the Stock Is Also a Buy for Retail Investors.

Sirius XM has performed well in 2026, and it has a deal in place that could generate even more meaningful revenue in the years ahead.

Berkshire Hathaway (BRKA +2.60%) (BRKB +1.41%) CEO Greg Abel's tenure is being defined by aggressive moves, with one of the most recent being the addition of more shares of Sirius XM Holdings (SIRI -1.32%) to the company's portfolio.

As revealed in a Form 4 filing, from Oct. 30 to Nov. 3, Berkshire purchased approximately $27 million worth of Sirius XM shares. By Berkshire's standards, that may sound small, with Sirius XM's weight in its portfolio at only 1.1%.

That said, the bigger vote of confidence from Abel's company is that it now owns 37.4% of the satellite radio provider. And as we head into 2027, investors may also want to consider Berkshire's moves and add the stock, or more of it, to their own portfolios.

Berkshire Hathaway CEO Greg Abel. Image source: Getty Images.

Over the last five years, Sirius XM has faced increased competition, a declining customer base, rising content costs, and a difficult market for acquiring new customers.

Heading into 2027 and beyond, while the stock price might not climb more than 60% each year, there's a reason Sirius XM could continue to be a long-term winner.

In April, Sirius XM struck a deal with Alphabet to become the exclusive advertising representative of YouTube's audio ad inventory in the United States. While YouTube was essentially just a platform to upload videos in its early days, it's become a more comprehensive destination for entertainment, ranging from live sports to podcasts to music. And it's a huge market for advertisers to reach. "According to a study from SiriusXM Media and Edison Research, there are more than 212 million monthly listeners in the U.S. engaging in audio-first content or environments on YouTube," Sirius said in a press release.

This deal won't be massively transformative right away, but by 2029, Deutsche Bank analysts estimate the partnership could generate $2 billion in incremental annual revenue for Sirius. For a company that generated $8.5 billion in 2025, that's meaningful.

If Sirius XM can set up other deals like this, it could ultimately become a profitable toll collector in the audio advertising space rather than competing in the crowded audio entertainment sector.

TL;DR: Rates fell today, but not by enough to change your mortgage math.

Mortgage rates are a little lower today. It probably won't last, thanks to new inflation data that has investors even more confident that the Federal Reserve will hike rates next month. You can read more on that below the charts.

Today, the average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage ticked down to 6.9% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is eight basis points lower than yesterday and 17 basis points lower than a week ago. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.)

Here are the average APRs we're seeing today, as well as movement over the past month for context:

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

This morning the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) dropped the October Consumer Price Index, which shows that inflation rose another 0.4% last month. This outpaced expectations: Economists had forecasted an increase of 0.3%. CPI is one of two key measures of inflation, which the Federal Reserve aims to keep in check relative to the strength of the labor market. (The Fed looks more closely at a different inflation measure, the Personal Consumption Expenditures Index, which comes out Nov. 25.)

Raising the federal funds rate is the Fed’s main tool for bringing inflation down, and futures traders are banking on a rate hike when the committee meets Dec. 8-9. The Fed doesn't set mortgage rates directly, but an anticipated rate hike can put upward pressure on mortgage rates, which respond to investors’ expectations for the economy and Fed policy.

Central bankers raised the federal funds rate in September, but it hasn’t been enough to pull inflation closer to the Fed’s target of 2%. Investors aren’t sure that one more hike in December will do the trick, either. According to CME FedWatch, further rate hikes may be in store for January.

» MORE: How the Federal Reserve affects mortgage rates

Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you plan to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs).

With rates where they are right now, you may want to start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.4% or higher.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

» Time to refi? Compare refinance rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

» Is now a good time to buy? See NerdWallet’s analysis

If you already have a quote you’re happy with, you should consider locking your mortgage rate, especially if your lender offers a float-down option. A float-down lets you take advantage of a better rate if the market drops during your lock period.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

🤓 Nerdy Reminder: Rates can change daily, and even hourly. If you’re happy with the deal you have, it’s okay to commit.

#3066. Resideo: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Management is betting on branded hardware over third-party OEM work, a shift that could reshape margins for years to come.

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 10, 2026, Resideo (REZI -2.99%) reported total revenue of $727 million, growing 3% year over year despite broader housing market headwinds. The company's post-spin focus as a stand-alone product business demonstrates how pricing power in core sales channels drives profitability. Three things management said stand out.

Resideo is scaling back its original equipment manufacturer (OEM) security business, in which it manufactures products for third parties that compete with its own brand at lower margins. Expanding higher-margin core sales channels protects profitability over the long term.

Management uses cost discipline and higher-priced product launches to expand margins. The resulting cash flows straight back into research and development (R&D), creating a self-sustaining growth cycle for its core home safety and heating, ventilation, and air conditioning (HVAC) products.

Following the August spin-off of ADI Distribution (ADI), its former security distribution arm, Resideo directed immediate capital allocation toward balance sheet health. Generating cash while shrinking debt lowers interest expense and improves financial flexibility.

Core channel momentum remains steady as product pipelines deliver. Management is countering input cost inflation through price increases and site consolidations while expanding software capabilities.

Software platform investments and core hardware focus support future expansion. Operational efficiency gains help fund engineering work.

#3065. Top Wall Street analysts believe in the growth potential of these 3 stocks

Geopolitical uncertainty in the Middle East and soaring bond yields weighed on global markets this past week. And investors are closely assessing the valuations of artificial intelligence stocks amid concerns about the sustainability of high spending on AI infrastructure.

Despite those continued challenges, top Wall Street analysts are bullish on the prospects of several stocks due to their long-run growth potential and exposure to lucrative business lines, including AI.

Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Cybersecurity company CrowdStrike Holdings (CRWD) is this week's first stock pick. The company is scheduled to announce fiscal second-quarter results on August 26.

Ahead of Q2 FY27 earnings, Truist analyst Junaid Siddiqui reiterated a buy rating on CrowdStrike stock and raised his price target to $245 from $187.50. Following CrowdStrike's impressive fiscal first-quarter performance and guidance raise, Siddiqui expects another strong quarter.

The 5-star analyst's optimism is backed by continued strength in Falcon Flex adoption and encouraging large deal activity. Siddiqui also cited continued momentum across emerging products. With the FY27 outlook assuming persistent strength in CrowdStrike's net new annual recurring revenue (ARR), Siddiqui is more focused on the longevity of key growth catalysts such as Falcon Flex adoption, platform consolidation and AI-led demand.

The analyst highlighted that talks with partners were encouraging, with pipeline generation and momentum in large deals remaining healthy in the fiscal second quarter despite tough, year-over-year comparisons.

"We continue to view CrowdStrike as one of the primary beneficiaries of platform consolidation, though we expect investors to remain focused on competitive dynamics and whether current growth levels represent a new baseline or a period of demand acceleration," the analyst said.

Siddiqui ranks No. 226 among more than 12,400 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 80% of the time, delivering an average return of about 40%. See CrowdStrike Financials on TipRanks.

Shares of personal computer maker Dell Technologies (DELL) have rallied 251% this year, driven by strong demand for AI servers. Recently, Evercore analyst Amit Daryanani reiterated a buy rating on DELL and raised his price target to $550 from $500.

The 5-star analyst contends that while Dell's AI compute segment is getting investors' attention, the company's Storage business is underappreciated and well-positioned to drive revenue and profit acceleration. Daryanani expects the storage business to see higher demand once enterprises start to bring workload back on-premises.

The analyst highlighted that Dell's Storage business, estimated to account for only 10% of FY27 revenue, is one of the factors that could help improve profit margins, given its higher profitability compared to AI servers. Daryanani estimates that the Storage business's operating margin is currently in the low-20% range, while margins for the AI server and traditional server businesses are in the mid-single-digit and mid-teens range, respectively.

Overall, Daryanani views the Storage business as an important catalyst for three reasons: Dell has one of the broadest storage portfolios in the industry; Storage has a significantly higher margin profile than AI servers; and the shift toward proprietary, software-defined storage and AI-focused platforms.

"We think DELL's storage business is becoming increasingly strategic as AI infrastructure deployments move beyond GPU procurement and toward full stack + AI-ready architectures," said Daryanani.

Daryanani ranks No. 19 among more than 12,400 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 71% of the time, delivering an average return of 38.70%. See Dell Technologies Statistics on TipRanks.

SanDisk (SNDK) is benefiting from AI-driven demand for its memory and storage products. Following the company's 2026 Investor Day event, J.P. Morgan analyst Harlan Sur resumed research coverage of SNDK with a buy rating (it was earlier, "Not Rated") and a price target of $2,250.

The 5-star analyst believes SanDisk is well-positioned to capitalize on a structural inflection reached in NAND demand, driven by strong growth in AI inference. Sur's bullishness is based on three key factors.

First, Sur believes that SanDisk's New Business Model (NBM) framework (or long-term agreements) has enhanced its margin profile and reduced cyclicality. SNDK's eight signed NBMs represent a total contract value of $94 billion and a gross margin of about 80%, even at the floor pricing.

Second, Sur highlighted the growing NAND market and expects the total addressable market to surge from about $70 billion in calendar year 2025 to over $300 billion in 2026 and about $500 billion in 2027. Importantly, the analyst noted that data centers are the largest driver of NAND growth, as hyperscalers increasingly deploy flash for AI inference workloads.

Finally, Sur is optimistic on SanDisk due to its technology dominance. The company's BiCS10 technology is sampling ahead of schedule and has 65% more bits per wafer than BiCS8, the analyst said. Also, Sur expects SanDisk's High Bandwidth Flash to become a differentiated memory platform for AI inference.

"Layered on top, mgmt's commitment to returning 100% of excess cash flow to shareholders should drive an aggressive share count reduction trajectory that further amplifies EPS growth on a per-share basis," said Sur.

Sur ranks No. 15 among more than 12,400 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 71% of the time, delivering an average return of 43.20%. See SanDisk Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

#3064. Car Insurance Soars for Drivers With Poor Credit; Here’s What to Do

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

While building your credit, shop around for auto insurance quotes. Some insurers are more lenient than others.

Lead Writer & Licensed Insurance Specialist

Your driving record may be spotless, but if you have poor credit, car insurance companies view you as a risk — and they’re significantly raising your rates.

Over the past three years, drivers with poor credit have seen auto insurance premiums surge 37.7%, according to NerdWallet’s 2026 Auto Insurance Rates Report. These price hikes were even steeper than those faced by drivers with good credit who caused a crash or got a DUI.

In January 2023, someone with poor credit and a clean driving record would pay a median of $2,864 per year for full-coverage car insurance, NerdWallet’s analysis found. By January 2026, premiums for this driver had risen to $3,944 — an increase of $1,081 per year. By comparison, the same driver with good credit saw an increase of only $576.

“Credit scores are one of the most harmful things that results in you paying higher auto insurance premiums,” says Michael DeLong, a research and advocacy associate with the Washington, D.C.-based nonprofit Consumer Federation of America. “The penalties are extremely severe.”

While higher premiums after a wreck or DUI may not be a surprise, DeLong says many drivers aren’t aware their credit scores will affect their car insurance rates. To further complicate things, building credit can take months.

But there are ways to get relief more quickly. DeLong suggests comparing car insurance quotes from multiple companies, because some insurers penalize poor credit less than others. Raising your deductible, evaluating your coverage and avoiding small claims can also help.

NerdWallet’s analysis found that insurers raised rates more sharply from 2023 to 2026 for drivers with poor credit than for those with good credit — even if the poor-credit driver had a flawless record while the good-credit driver had a DUI, speeding ticket or at-fault crash.

When our sample driver with poor credit also had a recent DUI or speeding ticket, rate increases were even greater. Prices for a full-coverage policy went up by more than 40% for drivers with poor credit and a recent DUI, the biggest increase of any profile we analyzed.

Drivers often think it’s unfair for credit to affect car insurance prices, DeLong says, since it isn’t directly linked to driving behavior. Some states agree; California, Hawaii and Massachusetts don’t allow credit as a factor in setting auto insurance rates.

However, insurers say credit scores can indicate the likelihood that a driver will file a claim.[1]National Association of Insurance Commissioners. Credit-Based Insurance Scores. Accessed Nov 2, 2026. View all sources They use what’s called a credit-based insurance score — similar to the typical credit scores used by lenders but weighted differently.

“It helps in predicting expected claims activity and loss costs more accurately,” said Norman Niami, a member of the American Academy of Actuaries' Automobile Insurance Committee, in an email.

The practice has been controversial, with critics arguing it disproportionately hurts low-income and minority drivers. But a Federal Trade Commission report to Congress in July 2007 concluded that credit-based insurance scores were strong predictors of risk even when controlled for income, race and ethnicity.[2]A Report to Congress by the Federal Trade Commission. Credit-Based Insurance Scores: Impacts on Consumers of Automobile Insurance. Accessed Nov 2, 2026. View all sources

The explanation may be that some people simply tend to take risks, according to a statistical analysis published in the North American Actuarial Journal in 2016.[3]North American Actuarial Journal. Empirical Evidence on the Use of Credit Scoring for Predicting Insurance Losses with Psycho-social and Biochemical Explanations. Accessed Nov 2, 2026. View all sources Researchers concluded that risk-taking behavior can affect credit scores as well as insurance claims. Their analysis found that average losses per policy were 64.6% higher for drivers with the lowest credit scores than for those with the best credit.

Working to build your credit over time may help lower your car insurance premiums, but it’s not a sure thing. A credit-based insurance score is just one of many factors (along with things like location, age and driving history) that insurers use to rate a person’s risk.

Building credit “can produce a noticeable premium decrease in some cases, while producing little or no change in others,” Niami said, depending on whether the new score causes an insurer to move you into a better rating tier. Each insurer sets its own score thresholds, so a score viewed as “poor” by one insurer might be considered “fair” by another.

At the same time, consumer advocates argue it’s difficult for many people to take the steps needed to strengthen their credit scores.

“Most people probably have some idea that you can improve your credit score by trying to pay your bills regularly and reliably, and using different kinds of financial resources and credit cards,” DeLong says.

“But again, that’s easier said than done," he says. "If you’re struggling at a low-wage job and trying to juggle bills, or if you don’t easily have access to a credit card, that advice may not be especially helpful."

Drivers with poor credit or no credit may be able to take other steps to lower their premiums.

Comparing car insurance quotes from different companies is one of the best ways to ensure you have the cheapest rate possible. Insurers set their own pricing formulas, and some are more forgiving of poor credit than others. A NerdWallet analysis of October 2026 rates found that in about half (49.3%) of U.S. ZIP codes in states that allow credit scoring, the cheapest insurer for a driver with poor credit was a different company than the cheapest for a driver with good credit.

Although you can’t improve your risk profile overnight, “there’s a bunch of small things you can do that over a two- to three-year span make you look a lot better” to insurers, says Bradley Flowers, founder of Portal Insurance agency in Mobile, Alabama.

Consider a higher deductible. Raising your car insurance deductible — the amount of a future claim that you agree to cover yourself — lowers your premium and signals to insurers that you’re less likely to file a claim. But be sure you can afford to pay the higher deductible if you have to make a claim.

Adjust how you’re billed by insurers. By signing up for automatic payments and ensuring you don’t miss insurance payments each month, you’ll get a small discount while improving your risk profile for insurers.

Avoid minor claims if you can. Flowers recommends thinking twice about filing minor claims, such as windshield cracks. “When you’re in one of these situations, let’s save our insurance for the really bad stuff,” he suggests.

Lastly, be sure your coverage fits your vehicle. If you could afford to replace your car on your own, consider dropping collision and comprehensive coverage to bring your premiums down. Your trimmed-down policy would still provide you with liability coverage after a crash, while leaving you to cover damage to your vehicle.

NerdWallet's 2026 Auto Insurance Rates Report is based on an analysis of more than 1.4 billion rate estimates provided by Quadrant Information Services for all 50 states and Washington, D.C., from January 2023 to January 2026.

Quadrant derives its rate data from modeled estimates based on carrier rating algorithms; figures do not reflect every available carrier or every consumer's individual rate. Liberty Mutual does not participate in Quadrant's rate data and is not represented in this analysis.

Quadrant’s figures are modeled rate estimates produced by running a fixed driver profile through carrier rating algorithms. They represent both new business and renewal rate estimates, and they are not a record of what actual drivers paid.

NerdWallet anchored its analysis to a 3-year old Toyota Camry LE, ensuring each analysis period reflected rates for the same-aged car.

The primary rate analysis is based on a 35-year-old single driver with good credit, no recent at-fault accidents or driving violations, and a full-coverage policy with $1,000 deductibles for collision and comprehensive coverage. Rates are pooled across male and female drivers.

In states where drivers must carry other types of insurance not included in our full coverage profile specifications, we added the minimum amount of coverage required by those states. Some policies include additional coverage at the insurer’s discretion.

In addition to our base profile driver with good credit and a spotless driving history, we analyzed rates for the following driver profiles:

Drivers with an at-fault crash. We added a single at-fault crash causing $10,000 in property damage.

Drivers with a speeding ticket. We added a single speeding ticket for driving 16 mph over the speed limit.

Drivers with a DUI. We added a single drunken-driving violation.

Drivers with poor credit. This is the same as our regular base profile, except the driver has poor credit instead of good credit. We also analyzed rates for drivers with poor credit and each of the three incidents above.

NerdWallet applied a strict comparability filter before calculating year-over-year figures. Only coverage variants and carrier/state combinations present in all four years of data were included in median calculations. This ensures reported changes reflect genuine pricing shifts among stable carriers, rather than differences caused by insurers entering markets, exiting, or going insolvent during the analysis period.

#3062. 1 Unstoppable AI Stock to Buy Hand Over Fist Before the Next Leg Higher

Iren's 70% crash does not align with its strengthening fundamentals. The mismatch won't provide an asymmetric opportunity forever.

Iren (IREN -7.85%) looks like a formidable AI stock to buy. Good stocks do not go down forever, and Iren has managed to improve its fundamentals despite dropping more than 70% from its all-time high. Recent earnings confirmed the bullish thesis, and broader neocloud trends have added fuel to the long-term picture.

Iren's business model involves building AI data centers, supplying infrastructure and cloud platforms, and renting out megawatts to hyperscalers and enterprises. As megawatts become more valuable, Iren's potential annual recurring revenue increases, and the company's recent earnings report hinted at this potential.

AI cloud revenue almost tripled sequentially to $200 million, which is a small slice of Iren's $20.3 billion revenue backlog. Operating annual recurring revenue has just crossed $1 billion, and the company intends to reach $4 billion by the end of January.

Notably, Iren secured a five-year deal at $22 million per megawatt and landed a short-term deal at $40 million per megawatt. Both of those figures are much higher than its landmark deal with Microsoft last year, which came in at $9.7 million per megawatt.

The value of a megawatt has more than doubled in less than one year. If that momentum continues, Iren will end up with far more lucrative deals in 2027. Leadership has also been very intentional about not rushing to sign new deals, which has proven to be the right call with each passing day.

Although October featured plenty of talk about neoclouds having less access to financing and being stuck with high interest rates, those issues don't concern Iren. Even the shareholder dilution concerns have faded after the company laid out its plan to raise capital.

Prepayments do the bulk of the work. The prepayment under the five-year deal, valuing each megawatt at $22 million, was sufficient to cover 90% of the associated GPU capital expenditures. That doesn't even include GPU financing, and Iren also has the flexibility to borrow against its data centers in the future.

Iren has no issue with raising the amount of funds it needs. This was a major bearish concern multiple months ago, especially stock dilution. Even though Iren has addressed this issue and strengthened its financial position, the growth stock remains well below its all-time highs. This mismatch is part of the reason Iren looks enticing at current levels.

As Iren delivers more megawatts and reports profitable quarters, funding its expansion will become even easier.

Although Iren has been quietly making more deals, it didn't add any additional sites this quarter, resulting in a 5.8-gigawatt portfolio. However, the company did unveil more than 35 gigawatts in its development pipeline. It demonstrates how quickly the tech company can add more gigawatts to its pipeline, but the conversion from developmental gigawatts to delivered power is not straightforward.

While Iren knows how to build data centers on time and on budget, the company acknowledged that its development projects are "speculative" and that a "significant portion" of them may not secure power. In other words, a large chunk of them will fall through.

Iren doesn't need all 35 of those gigawatts online to become a juggernaut. Even if it just adds 10 gigawatts from this development pipeline, Iren ends up with roughly 15.8 gigawatts. At $20 million per megawatt, that translates into more than $300 billion in annual recurring revenue.

Iren is at the center of the artificial intelligence boom. Neoclouds like Iren and Nebius (NBIS -5.27%) may be just as important as AI chipmakers in scaling out this new technology.

#3059. Forget the Market's Hottest Stocks. This Boring Dividend Stock Is Where I'd Put $1,000 Before 2027.

The market environment for the foreseeable future could be very different than it's been in the recent past.

After last week's sizable stumble, artificial intelligence stocks seem to be stabilizing, perhaps regrouping for a recovery. The AI trade appears to be back on.

Still, I'm not overly interested in adding more exposure to the AI sliver of the market while it's discounted. Last week's sell-off shows some vulnerability on this front, and perhaps for most of the overall stock market now that it's about as expensive as it's been in many years. We may be moving into a period where a surer thing is the smarter thing, including reliable income.

To this end, while it's admittedly boring, if I had an extra $1,000 to put to work right now, I'd use it to take on a position in the mundane grocery store chain The Kroger Company (KR +0.87%), plugging into its just-mediocre forward-looking yield of 2.3%. This often-ignored outfit has a very bullish secret.

You almost certainly know the company, perhaps better than you realize. While most of its nearly 2,800 grocery stores peppered across the United States operate under the Kroger banner, the company is also parent to Fred Meyer, Ralphs, Pick 'n Save, Marianos, and King Soopers, just to name a few. There's a good chance you've shopped at a Kroger-owned store without even realizing it, contributing to last year's revenue growth of 2.9% to $147.6 billion, more than $4.9 billion of which was turned into operating profit. That's not huge growth or a particularly wide profit margin rate, although by grocery store standards, it is.

This company delivers more shareholder value growth than it seems like it should be able to, however. While its top-line growth is usually only in the low single digits, over the course of the past 10 years, Kroger's dividend has grown by an average of 12.5%, from $0.12 then to $0.39 per share now. That's enormous dividend growth for any industry.

Granted, stock buybacks helped -- a lot. Since 2016, the grocer's outstanding share count has been dialed back from 959 million to 608 million as of the middle of this year, helping its annual earnings improve from $2.06 per share then to $4.85 per share now.

That's far from being a misleading metric, though. The Kroger Company earned enough real accessible cash during this stretch to fund these generous stock repurchases and pay its dividends.

This might put things in their proper perspective with this boring dividend stock: Had you made a $10,000 investment in KR stock 10 years ago and reinvested any dividends it dished out along the way, today your position would be worth $26,870, with most of that gain coming from -- surprisingly enough -- the stock's price appreciation rather than dividends. Your position would also be generating more than $600 worth of annual dividend income, by the way, to do with whatever you wish.

Then there's the simple fact that Kroger sells products that people must purchase over and over again, regardless of their price.

Obviously, there's no guarantee that the next 10 years will be as fruitful for Kroger's shareholders as the past 10 have been. In fact, there's a reasonably good chance they won't be. The grocer's considerably bigger now than it was then, so opportunities for future growth are (relatively) smaller in size and fewer in number. The stock's price has also nearly doubled during this time, dampening the benefit of its stock buybacks. Be sure to keep any expectations in check.

Still, while past performance is no guarantee of future results, the past is a reasonably good indication of how well a company functions, which points to the plausible future. All the attributes that made KR such a high-performance ticker for the past decade are still in place, and likely to continue growing this stock's value, even if at a slower pace.

More than anything, though, I'm starting to think the market environment is shifting toward a slower-moving one that's less charged by AI enthusiasm, making cash-generating names like Kroger all the more valuable. I don't want to simply shed all of my more aggressive growth holdings here. However, with interest rates already high and still rising, I do think it's time to prepare for a bit more economic lethargy. That means more reliable -- and growing -- cash flow, since the returns on other types of investments may be on the verge of weakening.

#3050. Coincheck: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Management's plan treats weak retail trading as a test of whether core operations can fund growth without new capital.

On its second-quarter fiscal 2027 earnings call, held on Nov. 9, 2026, Coincheck (CNCK -11.90%) detailed a three-phase operational plan to turn its core trading platform into a self-funding cash engine. Long-term investors need to evaluate whether the business can build lasting enterprise value as retail trading activity slows. Three takeaways from management's comments illustrate how the business plans to navigate this market shift.

Management is setting strict margin benchmarks across its core marketplace and asset management units so cash flow directly covers new product rollouts. This disciplined framework reduces reliance on external debt or equity dilution while retail trading volumes remain depressed.

The company is winding down Aplo, its European institutional brokerage subsidiary, to cut costs and integrate its trading technology into 3iQ, its Canadian digital asset management subsidiary. Reallocating those assets enables 3iQ to launch a separately managed account (SMA) product line for institutional clients in the first half of calendar 2027.

To offset lower spot crypto trading volumes in Japan, management launched contracts for differences (CFDs), which are leverage-based derivative products, in September 2026. Expanding into leveraged products and crypto-as-a-service partnerships positions the platform to capture demand from both institutional and retail investors as Japanese regulations evolve.

Trading activity across the crypto market remains muted, but management isn't waiting for market sentiment to recover before executing its long-term plan. The company holds key regulatory licenses in Japan, strong distribution partnerships with major financial firms, and an established institutional asset manager in 3iQ. Management focuses on strict margin benchmarks and efficient capital allocation across every operating unit.

By connecting its Japanese distribution network with 3iQ's institutional asset management capabilities, the business aims to create a repeatable platform that expands internationally once local operations generate consistent cash flow.

#3043. Bad News: There's a New Red Flag Ahead of the Anthropic IPO

The bond market has a can’t-miss warning for investors in artificial intelligence (AI) stocks.

Five months ago, on June 12, Elon Musk's Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX +0.72%), better known as SpaceX, rewrote Wall Street's record books with its $1.77 trillion initial public offering (IPO). In mere weeks, the developer of the Claude large language model (LLM), Anthropic (Nasdaq: ANT), may challenge SpaceX for the top spot with its own IPO.

Anthropic filed its public registration statement (S-1) on Oct. 26, starting the 15-calendar-day clock until it markets its upcoming debut and (likely) kicks off an IPO roadshow. With a lightning-fast growth rate that had Anthropic generating $65 billion in annual run rate sales as of July, there should be plenty of excited retail investors.

But skepticism is also building ahead of this monumental IPO. On top of a laundry list of historical headwinds, a new red flag has emerged ahead of Anthropic's debut.

Though history is an ally of long-term-minded investors, it can be the foe of IPOs and hyped tech trends, at least over shorter timelines.

For instance, every game-changing tech innovation since the mid-1990s has navigated an early-stage bubble-bursting event. These bubbles form and subsequently burst because investors overestimate how quickly game-changing tech innovations will be optimized. Consistently overshooting the mark leaves hyped technologies, including artificial intelligence (AI), prone to a bubble-bursting event.

Moral of the story - do NOT chase hot IPOs Year-1 average drawdown = 55% Year-1 median drawdown = 54% Table: Truist

Additionally, tech-focused IPOs don't have the best track record early on. Data from Truist Financial (TFC -0.14%) shows that the average year-one maximum drawdown for the 30 hottest tech-driven IPOs since May 2012 is 55%! SpaceX, which debuted after Truist released its data set, has endured a max drawdown of 54%!

History also says that premium valuations aren't well tolerated by Wall Street. For example, a trailing 12-month (TTM) price-to-sales (P/S) ratio above 30 can alert investors to an unsustainable bubble. Anthropic's TTM P/S ratio should land between 75 and 100 at its IPO.

The bad news for retail investors is that historical precedent isn't the only problem for Anthropic. The bond market is increasingly signaling that trouble lies ahead for AI hardware providers, neoclouds, and hyperscalers.

While some companies are financing the AI infrastructure build-out and the development of LLMs with cash on hand, most are relying on debt in some capacity. When public companies issue debt, they do so at a par value of $1,000, which is commonly expressed as $1 on financial websites. When bond traders are confident a company will make good on its debt obligations, the bond price hovers around par value.

Credit markets are flashing WARNING SIGNS across the AI trade: Oracle, $ORCL, 5-year credit default swap (CDS) spread has surged to ~263 basis points, while SpaceX's has risen to ~203 basis points, both at record highs. At the same time, CoreWeave's $CRWV, 5-year CDS is up to a record 982 basis points. This comes as tech companies have issued nearly $500 billion in new debt this year to finance AI infrastructure, with 9 US investment-grade bond deals worth at least $25 billion each. The growing debt burden is colliding with uncertainty over whether AI revenues will justify the enormous spending. As a result, investors are increasingly demanding higher compensation to take on credit risk. Oracle's market-implied 5-year default risk has risen above 20%, compared with around 16% for SpaceX and more than 7% for Nvidia. The pressure could intensify further, with Goldman Sachs projecting hyperscaler debt issuance to jump from $250 billion in 2026 to a massive $420 billion in 2027, as 35% of next year's capital spending is expected to be debt-funded. The AI boom is now testing credit markets, as investors begin repricing the risks behind Big Tech's unprecedented borrowing spree.

What we're seeing is several mid- and long-duration bond prices for AI companies plunging. The 2056 note SpaceX issued at par less than five months ago is trading at an all-time low of $0.83. Even Nvidia's (NVDA -5.47%) 2060 notes are trading at just $0.63.

The rout we've witnessed in bond prices, which has driven up yields, indicates tangible skepticism about the ability of AI companies to meet their debt obligations.

Given that Anthropic's operating model isn't yet time-tested or proven, this bond market malaise can sink Wall Street's hottest upcoming IPO before it has any chance to gain traction.

#3040. The 'debasement trade' returns after Bessent bond maneuver. Crypto and gold are back in style

The debasement trade is gaining new traction on Wall Street as concern over the size and cost of the budget deficit mounts.

The conventional wisdom behind the trade is that perceived hard assets, like cryptocurrencies and precious metals, gain as investors try to hedge against a weaker U.S. dollar and Treasury debt in the face of ballooning government spending. Those fears reached a fever pitch last week before, and after, the Treasury Department's unusual step of increasing debt buybacks under Secretary Scott Bessent.

"The size of the Treasury purchases announced so far by Bessent are trivial in comparison to the size of the overall market, but the [signaling] effect was very powerful," said Stephen Coltman, head of macro at 21Shares, a crypto-focused creator of exchange-traded funds.

Gold touched three-month highs Monday, building on last week's advance of more than 5%. The yellow metal has climbed for five straight weeks and in August is on track for its biggest monthly rise since 1999.

Bitcoin added 2% Monday, to the highest since May. Last week, the digital currency soared 22%, its biggest three-day rally since 2023. Overnight Tuesday, the crypto touched $80,000.

The U.S. dollar index, which tracks the dollar against six other leading currencies, hit three-month lows last week and recorded its third down week in the last four. The index was little changed on Monday as investors expressed little appetite to bid up the greenback.

The Treasury Department said last week that it would double the maximum size of its bond buyback, to at least $4 billion from $2 billion. Two senior Treasury officials told CNBC Monday that the department could use its General Account to help fund the plans.

Last week's announcement followed news that the monthly U.S. budget deficit in July reached a five-year high and came at the same time as total federal government debt topped $40 trillion. Bessent told CNBC last week that he wields a "big toolkit" to calm the government bond market amid concerns about the government's financial health.

Long-dated U.S. Treasury yields surged last week, at one point sending the 30-year yield to almost a 20-year high of 5.34%, up from 4.82% in late June. Yields dipped and then rebounded in the wake of the Treasury buyback move, a signal that bond investors believed Bessent's moves were inadequate.

"Markets are saying something," the billionaire philanthropist and former energy trader John Arnold said in a Friday post on X. The weaker dollar, lower Treasury prices and strengthening hard assets, are "all part of the debasement trade," he wrote.

The Treasury's moves could aid the bond market, but also translate into outsized pain for the dollar, according to Nohshad Shah, Citadel Securities' head of fixed income sales for Europe, the Middle East and Africa.

The stakes are high for monetary policymakers, as a weaker greenback can ease financial conditions, Shah said. U.S. inflation — above the Federal Reserve's 2% target for five years — could worsen.

The Fed might need to hike interest rates in response, Shah said. Fed funds futures reflect about a 56% chance the central bank raises borrowing costs at its October meeting, up more than seven percentage points from a week ago, according to CME's FedWatch tool.

"The bond market's message is straightforward: fiscal or monetary policy should be tighter," Shah said in a Monday note. "Households may ultimately pay for policymakers' unwillingness to fix the roof whilst the sun is shining."

Coltman at 21Shares said the appetite for alternative stores of value also stems from mounting geopolitical tension. The U.S. on Monday rolled out a global sanctions program focused on segregating Iran from the global economy, days after slapping 50% tariffs on billions of dollars in Canadian exports.

Still, assets that would benefit from a debasement trade have recently received votes of confidence on Wall Street.

Deutsche Bank analyst Michael Hsueh said in a Monday note that gold could surpass his target price of $4,800 an ounce. Already, that level suggests the precious metal only need to rise another 3% or so from where it closed on Friday. "We see the Treasury policy change as underlining the gold constructive view," Hsueh said.

Billionaire investor Ray Dalio recommended investors remain overweight gold and bitcoin ahead of what he warned could become a debt crisis in the U.S. as a result of unchecked government spending. Gold could account for as much as 15% of a model portfolio, the Bridgewater Associates founder said.

"The government's financial condition is at an inflection point," Dalio wrote on LinkedIn Friday. "If this is not dealt with now, the debts will build up to levels where they can't be managed without great trauma."

Others are less sure, devaluing the notion of a debasement trade.

It's probably too early to endorse the idea unless it's clear that the Fed will go along with the Treasury Department, said Alexander Lis, investing chief at Social Discovery Ventures.

#3038. This Fast-Growing Insurance Stock Is About to Do Something It's Never Done Before

Lemonade expects its first quarter of positive adjusted EBITDA, and its growth is speeding up at the same time.

For most of its time as a public company, the knock on Lemonade (LMND -1.73%) has been simple. It grows fast, but it loses a lot of money doing it. That's about to change, at least by one important measure.

In its third-quarter earnings report, Lemonade said that it expects to generate positive adjusted EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization) in the fourth quarter for the first time. This is a major milestone, and it's one that shareholders have been waiting for. With that in mind, here's a rundown of Lemonade's numbers, its profitability claims, and what investors should keep in mind as we head into 2027.

The best measure of Lemonade's growth is in-force premium, the annualized value of all the insurance policies it has in place. In the third quarter, this figure grew 34% year over year to $1.55 billion, an acceleration from growth in the low 30s over the previous four quarters. Other growth metrics look excellent as well. For example, Lemonade now has 3.52 million customers, 23% more than a year ago.

Lemonade's revenue grew even faster, up 73% year-over-year to $336.1 million. However, a big part of that came from Lemonade passing less of its business to reinsurers, which means it keeps more premium (and more risk) on its own books. That's one big reason why it's smart to focus on in-force premium instead.

The car insurance business is a big part of the momentum. This is both Lemonade's largest growth opportunity (by far), as well as one of its big risk factors, as auto insurance is highly competitive. But the news was great. In-force premium from Lemonade Car rose to $265 million from $163 million a year ago, and the product is now available in 14 states.

Lemonade's adjusted EBITDA was a loss of $20.4 million in the third quarter, but management expects a positive $5 million to $9 million in the fourth quarter and its first full year of positive adjusted EBITDA in 2027. The plan is to grow marketing and other growth spending more slowly than in-force premium from here, so this figure should get significantly larger in the future.

It's also worth noting that Lemonade already generates cash. Adjusted free cash flow was $27 million in the third quarter and $63.2 million through the first nine months of the year. But adjusted EBITDA is a more widely recognized metric of profitability, and helps provide an easier comparison with other companies that also report this figure.

To be sure, adjusted EBITDA isn't the same as profit, and Lemonade still reported a net loss of $0.56 per share. A big reason why is the company's stock-based compensation, which is on the high end and has been for Lemonade's entire publicly traded history. Interest expense has also been elevated recently.

Plus, Lemonade's gross loss ratio, the share of premiums paid out in claims, rose to 65% from 62% a year ago, which is still significantly below Lemonade's 75% stated target. Over the past 12 months, it was a much better 60%, but insurance results can swing from quarter to quarter, especially when catastrophes hit. Keeping more risk on its own books also means a bad quarter would hurt more than it used to. And car insurance is a tough, competitive business.

Having said all that, Lemonade is growing faster while spending less to do it, and it's on the verge of the profitability milestone that many skeptics said it would never reach. I'm holding my shares, and the fourth-quarter results will be the first test of whether this turnaround is for real.

#3035. Alphabet or CoreWeave: Which AI Stock Is Better to Buy in a Market Crash?

Alphabet and CoreWeave are both positioned to benefit from AI, but one has a much stronger financial foundation.

A stock market crash can create opportunities to buy great businesses at discounted prices. But in the artificial intelligence boom, which stock should investors consider: Alphabet (GOOGL -0.27%) (GOOG -0.38%) or CoreWeave (CRWV -0.51%)?

Both companies stand to benefit from growing demand for AI. However, they offer very different investment opportunities.

Alphabet owns some of the world's most valuable technology businesses and is investing heavily in AI. CoreWeave provides the computing infrastructure needed to develop and run AI models.

If I could choose only one during a market crash, I would favor Alphabet. It offers exposure to AI through several established businesses, providing investors with a stronger financial foundation amid uncertain economic conditions.

Alphabet is more than a search engine company. Google Search, YouTube, and Google Cloud provide several revenue streams. These businesses also give Alphabet an enormous customer base through which it can distribute AI products and services.

The company's latest results demonstrate this strength. In the third quarter of 2026, revenue increased 25% year over year to $127.6 billion. Operating income rose 30% to $40.6 billion, while Google Cloud revenue more than doubled to $30.7 billion.

The important point is that Alphabet isn't relying entirely on AI to grow. Google Search and YouTube already generate substantial revenue, while Google Cloud benefits as businesses adopt AI. This gives Alphabet several ways to participate in the AI opportunity. It can monetize AI through advertising, cloud computing, subscriptions, and its own AI models.

There are risks, of course. AI could change how people search for information, potentially challenging Google's traditional advertising business. Alphabet is also spending heavily on data centers and computing infrastructure, which could put pressure on cash flow if returns disappoint.

Nevertheless, its established businesses provide a financial cushion that many smaller AI companies lack.

CoreWeave is a different kind of AI investment. Instead of developing consumer products or search engines, it provides specialized cloud infrastructure that allows businesses to train and run AI models.

As AI adoption grows, demand for computing power could increase substantially. CoreWeave wants to capture a portion of that demand. Its second -quarter 2026 results were impressive. Revenue increased 112% year over year to $2.6 billion, while its revenue backlog reached approximately $104 billion. That backlog suggests strong customer demand, although it represents future contracted business rather than cash already received.

Still, the biggest problem is that building AI infrastructure requires enormous amounts of capital. CoreWeave's capital expenditures reached approximately $9.4 billion in the second quarter alone. It also recorded an adjusted net loss of $567 million. This creates a financial vulnerability.

If AI customers reduce spending or financing becomes more expensive, CoreWeave could struggle to fund its expansion. Its equipment also requires continual investment as newer generations of chips become available.

In short, the company could become a major winner if AI demand continues expanding. But investors must recognize that its growth depends on substantial capital investment and continued access to financing.

The difference between these companies becomes particularly important during an economic downturn. Imagine that businesses become more cautious about AI spending. Both companies could experience slower growth, but their financial positions would give them different levels of flexibility.

Alphabet has established businesses generating substantial operating profits. It can continue investing in AI even if demand temporarily weakens. CoreWeave has a more concentrated business model and much higher financing requirements relative to its scale. A slowdown could affect not only its growth prospects but also its ability to fund new infrastructure.

That doesn't mean CoreWeave will fail. Its enormous backlog and relationships with major customers demonstrate meaningful demand. But the company's financial risks are considerably higher.

For investors, this distinction matters. A market crash could make either stock cheaper. But the objective during a market crash shouldn't simply be to buy the stock that has fallen the most. It should be to identify businesses capable of emerging from the downturn stronger.

Both Alphabet and CoreWeave could benefit enormously from the AI revolution. But I would approach them differently. Alphabet is my choice for investors seeking long-term AI exposure with a stronger underlying business. CoreWeave is a more speculative opportunity for investors comfortable with substantial financial and execution risks.

A market crash could make either stock cheaper. But investors should still examine their valuations rather than assume a large share-price decline automatically creates a bargain. When investing in a promising industry, sometimes the best opportunity isn't the company with the most exciting growth. It's the company with the financial strength to keep winning when conditions become difficult.

#3031. Interactive Brokers Group vs. Mastercard: Which Financial Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

Interactive Brokers trades at a lower forward P/E than Mastercard, but their balance sheets and margins tell very different stories.

Investors often weigh high-growth companies against established giants. Comparing Interactive Brokers Group (IBKR +0.03%) and Mastercard (MA +0.46%) reveals two different ways to potentially build wealth in the global financial markets.

Interactive Brokers Group focuses on low-cost execution for sophisticated, active traders and institutions around the world. Mastercard operates one of the largest payment networks, facilitating trillions of dollars in annual transaction volume. Both companies are central to modern finance, but they serve different roles for retail and institutional clients.

This company provides direct-access trade execution and clearing services for a diverse group of clients. It serves approximately 4.4 million cleared customer accounts, including hedge funds, mutual funds, and individual investors. Interactive Brokers focuses on automation and low costs to attract active participants as one of the leading financial stocks in the global market.

In fiscal 2025, revenue reached nearly $6.2 billion, representing growth of approximately 19.7% compared to the previous year. This performance helped the company generate net income of roughly $984 million. Interactive Brokers achieved a net margin of close to 15.9%, up from about 14.6% in the prior fiscal period, reflecting its ability to scale its low-cost model effectively.

According to its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is 0, indicating the company has no debt relative to its shareholders' equity. The current ratio, which measures the ability to pay short-term obligations with short-term assets, sits at approximately 1.1. Free cash flow for fiscal 2025 was nearly $15.7 billion, representing cash from operations minus capital expenditures.

This payments leader operates a technology-driven network that connects consumers, merchants, and financial institutions in more than 220 countries and territories. It earns fees by processing transactions and providing value-added services like data analytics and security. Mastercard relies on deep partnerships with banks and digital companies to facilitate its global reach.

In fiscal 2025, revenue reached nearly $32.8 billion, a 16.4% increase over the previous year. This robust top-line performance translated into net income of about $15 billion. The company maintained a high net margin of approximately 45.6%, which highlights its ability to convert a significant portion of every dollar earned into profit.

As of Mastercard's December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is roughly 2.5. The current ratio is approximately 1, indicating its short-term assets are roughly equal to its short-term liabilities. Free cash flow for the fiscal year ended in 2025 reached nearly $16.4 billion.

Interactive Brokers Group faces risks from its concentrated ownership structure, as Chairman Thomas Peterffy holds voting control. The business is heavily dependent on its proprietary technology and automation, making it vulnerable to technical failures or systemic market events. It also faces global regulatory scrutiny and competition from other digital brokerage platforms.

Interactive Brokers Group appears more attractively priced based on its forward P/E, which compares stock price to future earnings estimates.

Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

How a stock has performed in the past does not necessarily predict how it will perform in the future. Still, I do think it's worth reviewing. Interactive Brokers and Mastercard went public almost exactly a year apart, in 2007 and 2006, respectively.

Mastercard shares have left both Interactive Brokers and the S&P 500 in the dust. The credit card giant also pays a modest dividend, which may appeal to some investors.

What I find most attractive about Mastercard is its high net margin. The ability to convert more than 45% of revenue into profits is impressive and would be the envy of most companies.

To be clear, I don't think Interactive Brokers is a bad stock. I just think the secular trend toward increasing use of digital payments is something Mastercard (and other payment specialists) will continue to benefit from. Because of these tailwinds, Mastercard gets my vote here.

Buying an exchange-traded fund (ETF) that tracks a diversified index like the S&P 500 is one of the surest ways to build wealth in the stock market over the long term. It's a strategy every investor should consider, no matter their age.

However, young investors in their 20s have time on their side, so they might be comfortable with a little more volatility in exchange for the opportunity to earn even higher returns. Having more exposure to companies developing revolutionary technologies like artificial intelligence (AI) could supercharge their portfolio over the long term.

The Roundhill Generative AI and Technology ETF (CHAT -1.12%) exclusively invests in the world's top AI stocks. It's down 35% from its June all-time high (as of the market close on Nov. 6), and if I were in my 20s today, here's why I'd take this opportunity to add it to my diversified portfolio.

The Roundhill Generative AI and Technology ETF is actively managed, which means rather than simply tracking an index, a team of professional portfolio managers regularly buy and sell stocks based on what they believe will produce the best returns. But they adhere to a criteria, investing only in companies developing the hardware infrastructure, software, and platforms powering the AI revolution.

The Roundhill ETF currently holds just 36 stocks, and it's quite top-heavy, because its five largest positions represent 31.5% of the value of its entire portfolio.

Data source: Roundhill Investments. Portfolio weightings are accurate as of Nov. 8, 2026, and are subject to change.

Nvidia is the world's largest semiconductor company. Its graphics processing units (GPUs) for the data center are the best chips in the industry for processing AI workloads, and it continues to experience more demand than it can supply. In fact, chief executive Jensen Huang says every frontier AI model company plans to adopt the new Vera Rubin GPU systems.

Alphabet, Microsoft, and Amazon operate the three largest cloud computing platforms in the world, where they give enterprise customers access to data center capacity, ready-made foundation models, and other tools that are essential for deploying AI software. Each of these companies also developed its own AI assistant, which it integrated into legacy software systems to unlock new revenue streams.

Meta Platforms is the parent company of the Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp social media applications. However, it launched a personal AI assistant called Muse in September which already has over 10 million users. It can do everything from managing the user's emails to handling their shopping, so it could significantly expand Meta's addressable market beyond social media.

Some of the other AI powerhouses in the Roundhill ETF include Advanced Micro Devices, Micron Technology, CrowdStrike, and Elon Musk's Space Exploration Technologies.

The Roundhill Generative AI and Technology ETF was established in May 2023, so it doesn't have a very long track record. However, even after losing one-third of its value over the last few months, the ETF has still returned 160% since its inception, more than twice the 75% return of the S&P 500 over the same period.

I think it will trend higher over the long term because the AI boom is still in its infancy. While chips and data centers are the primary drivers of value right now, technologies like robotics and autonomous vehicles could be orders of magnitude larger in the future. But given its highly concentrated exposure to the AI industry alone, investors shouldn't bet the farm on the Roundhill ETF.

Had an investor parked $20,000 in an S&P 500 index fund in May 2023, they would have roughly $35,000 today. But had they put 70% of that money in the S&P and the other 30% in the Roundhill ETF, they would be sitting on $40,100 today instead. That demonstrates how an investor can use the ETF alongside a traditional index fund to supercharge their returns.

But remember, that strategy will come with added volatility. Not every investor would be comfortable with seeing a particular asset decline by 35% in just a few months, so while I would buy this ETF with the intention of holding it forever if I were in my 20s, it certainly isn't for everyone.

#3018. Believe it, Lakers are NBA championship contenders

Luka Dončić is playing as though he's on a revenge tour and every opposing player has former Mavericks general manager Nico Harrison's face superimposed on it.

Austin Reaves is playing as though he were shortchanged by signing a four-year, $180 million deal over the summer, the richest contract in NBA history for a player who went undrafted.

Los Angeles Lakers guard Luka Doncic (77) shoots against Atlanta Hawks guard CJ McCollum during an NBA game, Monday, Nov. 9, 2026, in Atlanta. AP Photo/Mike Stewart

Walker Kessler is playing as though he's hellbent on fulfilling his vow to "run through a wall" for the Lakers after they emptied their treasure trove of draft capital to acquire him in July.

And the Lakers' role players are playing as though they deeply understood the assignment when they joined a 17-time championship franchise.

The Lakers have the league's best record at 10-2. They've won six games in a row.

That isn't a sentence we thought we'd write heading into this season. Not with nine new players. Not with so many question marks around their perimeter defense. Not with their lack of depth at backup center.

But now, Lakers general manager Rob Pelinka looks like the Albert Einstein of basketball rosters and coach JJ Redick looks like a superstar whisperer.

The Lakers last won a championship in 2020, their first title in 10 years.

They could snap their six-year drought this season.

Dončić is on a historic tear, averaging 39.3 points (49.8% shooting from the field, 40.7% from beyond the arc), 7.8 rebounds, 7.9 assists and two steals per game.

In his first nine games of the season, Dončić scored 361 points, surpassing Michael Jordan's 347 points in 1986-87 for the most points scored through that period in modern NBA history.

But what really made the Lakers look like contenders is how they played without Dončić (lower back tightness) on Sunday against the Pistons.

Austin Reaves (15) of the Los Angeles Lakers reacts after a late second-half 3-point basket against the Detroit Pistons in Detroit, Sunday, Nov. 8, 2026. Getty Images

Without the league's current front-runner for the MVP Award and against a Pistons team with the third-highest defensive rating, Reaves scored a season-high 43 points in the Lakers' 121-116 win.

He reminded everyone of what he can do when he's unleashed.

Reaves has quietly been putting together a spectacular season. He's averaging 25.3 points on a very efficient 50.8% from the field and 41.3% from beyond the arc.

He's the 15th leading scorer in the league, and of those ahead of him, only Giannis Antetokounmpo, Anthony Davis and Victor Wembanyama have higher field-goal percentages than Reaves.

And only Jamal Murray and Steph Curry are shooting at a higher percentage from beyond the 3-point line.

Dončić and Reaves are the NBA's highest-scoring duo by a mile, averaging 64.6 points, 12.6 more than the second-leading duo of Steph Curry and Yaxel Lendeborg, who are averaging a combined 52 points per game.

Then there's Kessler, who's averaging a double-double with 14.9 points and 10.8 rebounds per game.

When Reaves was out for Monday's 124-114 win over the Hawks because of an illness, Dončić got help from the Lakers' reserves, with Collin Sexton having an 18-point, six-assist performance and Sandro Mamukelashvili pouring in 23 points and grabbing eight rebounds.

Los Angeles Lakers center Walker Kessler (14) shoots against Atlanta Hawks center Jock Landale (31) during an NBA basketball game, Monday, Nov. 9, 2026, in Atlanta. AP Photo/Mike Stewart

The Lakers have the highest offensive rating in the league at 121.5. And even though they're 19th in defensive rating (113.8), they rank second in the league in steals per game (10.8), second in total deflections (240) and third in blocks per game (6.4).

Kessler leads the NBA in contested shots (140).

Heck, even Dončić, who has notoriously been slammed for his defense throughout his career, is showing a lot of effort on the less glamorous end of the court. He leads the league in defensive loose balls recovered (nine) and is tied for second in charges drawn (four).

Entering this season, it was presumed that the Lakers needed time to jell. It seemed as though they had major holes. They weren't ready to compete with the league's elite teams, such as the Thunder, Spurs or Knicks.

The Lakers have sprinted past their doubters, proving that they're a team to watch.

#3017. Breakfast News: Unity Software – Measure Twice!

Why a Unity buyout deserves a higher valuation, CoreWeave shrugs off debt jitters, and more…

Silver Lake and Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund have reportedly held talks to acquire Unity Software (U -2.12%), and we understand why.We first recommended Unity ("The U") in Hidden Gems at $17.09 in September 2024. We've made 22 additional recommendations and investments since then and have not sold a share. Today, the stock is at $50.34.Let's remind ourselves what Unity Software does and then consider the buyout together.

Unity makes the software that developers use to build video games, especially on phones. It also runs an ad business that helps those games find players.

CEO Matt Bromberg (a throwback all the way to America Online in 1999 – Motley Fool memories!) joined in May 2024 and inherited a company at war with those developers. He fixed that first, scrapping the controversial runtime fee and winning them back. He then rebuilt the company's ad business around Vector, an AI engine.Last quarter, these efforts produced Unity's first GAAP profit since going public in 2020, on top of 32% revenue growth. Its Vector ad engine grew 126% year over year.

Vector's edge comes from data. Roughly three billion people play Unity-built games each month, and what happens inside those games now trains Vector's AI. More than 90% of new Unity projects opt in to sharing in-game data. Few rivals see inside the game itself. That advantage is a multiplier.

And that's what attracts this investor consortium. It already owns major gaming businesses like Electronic Arts and Scopely. Owning Unity could deepen that integration, improving game development, player acquisitions, and advertising profitability across the broader portfolio.Silver Lake has an excellent reputation as a long-term partner. The firm made its first investment into Unity Software in 2017, and its CEO Egon Durban joined the company's board then as well. (Of course, that board seat also complicates this negotiation.)Early reports suggest a first valuation of $25 billion (around $55 per share). To our eye, that doesn't adequately reflect the value emerging in Unity's advertising business.What buyout price would we support? $75.04 per share.Vector is taking market share in a competitive environment, and its existing advertising customers are increasing their spend. Unity Software has a path to generating gross margins in the mid-80s percent alongside returns on invested capital in the mid-teens.

You could, therefore, in just a few years, find this company driving double-digit top line growth with rising margins and capital efficiency, generating over $2 billion in free cash flow. Our ballpark $33 billion price is more valid than the aforementioned $25 billion.And as long-term business owners in Fooldom, we're very happy to keep holding our shares in an independent U!

The artificial intelligence (AI) trade just got two very different signals. CoreWeave’s (CRWV -0.51%) debt-fueled expansion, a brutal sell-off in its stock and bonds, and questions about whether AI demand can justify the spending rattled investors. The AI cloud provider’s latest earnings offered some reassurance, sending Nasdaq futures up 1.4% this morning. CoreWeave popped over 10% in pre-market trading.

But there's a wrinkle: while demand for AI computing remains red-hot, investors appear less willing to pay absolutely anything for a piece of the boom.

Have you ever rooted against a buyout of a company you owned? Which one, and why?
